title: Stage III: Planning the Way Forward
overview: Chapter 13 covers Stage III of Egan's problem-management model, which turns Stage II goals into a practical 'game plan'. It distinguishes action, outcome and impact (the case of Lacy), sets out the three tasks of Stage III, and revisits Mara's goals. Task III-A covers developing possible strategies through focused brainstorming, prompt and fade, resource frameworks (the case of Jackson) and skills training. Task III-B covers choosing best-fit strategies: Bud's odyssey, criteria for strategies (specific, effective, realistic, value-consistent), strategy sampling, the balance-sheet method, linking strategies to action, and the shadow side of decision making, including three risk pitfalls. Task III-C covers formulating plans: Frank's failure to plan, how plans add value, shaping plans (Harriet, Frank revisited), and four principles for humanising constructive change. The chapter ends with ready-made programmes: evidence-supported treatments and general well-being programmes.
objectives: Explain the broad and narrow meanings of planning and distinguish action, outcome and impact.
Describe the three tasks of Stage III and how they relate to Figure 13.1.
Explain the principles for helping clients discover viable strategies, including brainstorming, prompt and fade, resource frameworks and skills training.
Apply the criteria for choosing best-fit strategies, strategy sampling and the balance-sheet method.
Identify the shadow side of selecting strategies, including Goslin's pitfalls and the three risk pitfalls.
Describe how plans add value and how to shape a plan by action, sequence and time frame.
Explain the four principles for humanising the mechanics of constructive change.
Outline ready-made action programmes, including ESTs and general well-being programmes, and Egan's both-and position.

sections.heading: The Three Tasks of Stage III
sections.detailed:
Planning in two senses. Egan says that, broadly understood, planning covers everything done in Stages II and III, so it concerns both big-S solutions (goals) and small-s solutions (the means to them). In the narrower sense used in this chapter, planning means identifying, choosing and organising the strategies required to reach goals. Stage II is about outcomes, goals that have been "powerfully imagined"; Stage III is about the activities or work that will produce those outcomes. It concerns "implementation intentions" and, eventually, implementation itself.

Action, outcomes and impact. Clients exploring what is going wrong often ask straight away what they should do. Egan accepts that action is essential, but it is valuable only to the extent that it produces problem-managing and opportunity-developing outcomes, and outcomes in turn matter only if they have a constructive impact on the client's life. The case of Lacy, a 40-year-old single woman, separates these ideas. Her actions (attending AA meetings, following the 12 steps, avoiding tempting situations, phoning fellow members when depressed or tempted) produce an outcome: over seven months of sobriety. The impact is that she feels better about herself and has the energy to make friends, join church activities and travel.

The contrast case within Lacy's life. Lacy is also in a psychologically abusive relationship; her drinking had partly been a way of avoiding it. She takes many actions: she becomes more assertive, cuts off contact when he turns abusive and stops letting him make all the decisions. Yet there is no satisfactory outcome, because she has never decided what outcome she wants, what kind of relationship she would like or whether to end it. Lots of activity without a defined goal leads nowhere. After a seriously abusive episode she ends the relationship (action), the relationship ends for good (outcome) and she feels liberated but lonely (impact). This new problem means the helping process must be recycled.

The three tasks. Stage III has three interrelated tasks, all aimed at problem-managing action by the client:
- Task III-A, possible strategies: help clients develop possible ways of reaching their goals ("What kind of actions will help me get what I need and want?").
- Task III-B, best-fit strategies: help clients choose strategies that are effective, efficient and suited to their preferences and resources ("What actions are best for me?").
- Task III-C, plans: help clients turn strategies into a realistic plan ("What should my campaign for constructive change look like? What first, what second, when do I start?").

Figure 13.1 shows these as reviewing possible strategies ("What are the paths to my goals?"), choosing the best fit ("What strategies make most sense for me?") and crafting a practical plan ("What does the way forward look like?"), all leading to ongoing action and problem-managing outcomes.

Planning is not action. Stage III supplies the final pieces of the client's programme, the "game plan". But the three tasks are planning for action and must not be confused with action itself. Without action, a constructive-change programme is only a wish list. Implementation is the subject of the next chapter.
sections.simple: Stage III is about working out how to reach the goals set in Stage II. Egan separates action (what the client does), outcome (what is achieved) and impact (how life improves), using the case of Lacy. Stage III has three tasks: list possible strategies, choose the best-fit ones, and turn them into a plan. Planning is not the same as acting; without action a plan is just a wish list.
keyPoints: Broad planning covers Stages II and III; narrow planning means identifying, choosing and organising strategies.
Stage II is about outcomes; Stage III is about the activities that produce them ('implementation intentions').
Action matters only if it leads to outcomes, and outcomes only if they have a constructive impact (case of Lacy).
Task III-A: possible strategies; Task III-B: best-fit strategies; Task III-C: plans (Figure 13.1).
Planning for action is not action; without action a change programme is a wish list.

sections.heading: Mara and Carlos Revisited: Mara's Goals
sections.detailed:
Where Mara stands. After the disastrous conversation with her father, Mara found herself back at Stage I and emotionally devastated. She slid into full-blown depression and needed some weeks, even with Carlos's help, to start recovering. She realised that her excitement about a better future had hidden from her how deep her father's opposition might go. She had not taken the rehearsals with Carlos seriously, because even when he played an angry father she saw him as Carlos, someone she liked and respected. Her mother offered some comfort but clearly sided with her husband, so apart from Carlos, Mara felt alone.

Plan B. As she regained balance, her immediate goal was to arrange a second conversation to learn whether her father would discuss her future, careers and social life with any openness. If not, she would need a Plan B. When she raised it, he calmly said he thought the matter was settled and they should both get on with their lives. Mara saw that building a better future was something she would have to do herself.

The crisis as energiser. Carlos had suspected an ongoing low-grade depression, but he noticed that the crisis somehow energised her. She still felt negative emotions at times but no longer seemed depressed; it was as if the crisis had swept away the cobwebs, leaving her freer and more determined.

Support community first. With Carlos's help she concluded that she might eventually have to break away from her parents, but for that she would need a support group, something like the young people she had met in Iran. The immediate need was a community that would know her, accept her aspirations and back her as she built a different life. With that in place she could tackle the harder task of creating a new career, even if it meant moving away.

Cultural tension. Leaving home would be daunting because her Iranian roots run deeper than she had thought, while the get-up-and-go side of American culture also appeals to her; the two sometimes work together and sometimes clash. She half-flirts with living in Iran, but with Carlos sees she has been idealising her trip. The upside would be a ready-made community; the downside is that her American side might clash with the Iranian system, and the young people she met complained a good deal about life there.

Mara's three goals.
1. Social life: how to establish or enter a community with something like the spirit she experienced in Iran.
2. Work life: what she must do to move to a better career.
3. Her arrangement with her parents: how to prepare to leave them, if that is the price of the other two goals, and what to do if her father falls ill, the business crashes or they reject her completely.

Egan concludes that Mara has plenty of work ahead, and Stage III is precisely about the work clients must do to manage problems and develop unused opportunities.
sections.simple: After her father refused to talk, Mara realised she must build her future herself, and the crisis actually energised her. She decided she first needed a supportive community before tackling a career change or leaving home. Her three goals are a better social life, a better career, and preparing to leave her parents if necessary.
keyPoints: Mara's failed talk with her father sent her back to Stage I and into depression for some weeks.
Her father declined further dialogue, so she needed a Plan B and to shape her future herself.
The crisis energised her; Carlos saw her as freer and more determined.
She saw a support community as the first step before career change or leaving home; she was idealising Iran.
Three goals: social life (community), work life (better career), and preparing to leave her parents.

sections.heading: Task III-A: Help Clients Develop Strategies for Accomplishing Their Goals
sections.detailed:
What strategies are. Egan defines strategies as actions that help clients accomplish their goals. The chapter matters because it deals with the actions clients must take to change their lives, which is why a bias toward action is one of the key helping values set out in Chapter 2.

An exercise in liberation. Developing a range of possible strategies is described as liberating. Clients who feel hemmed in by their problems and unsure whether their goals are workable are freed when they define a way forward. Seeing clear pathways to goals increases self-efficacy: "I can do this."

Strategy and adverse conditions. Strategy is the art of identifying and choosing realistic courses of action for reaching goals, and of doing so under adverse conditions such as war. Clients' problem situations are themselves adverse conditions; clients are often at war with themselves and the world. Helping them develop strategies can therefore be a thoughtful, humane and fruitful way of being with them.

A step helpers avoid. Egan notes that some helpers skip this step because it seems jargon-laden and mechanical. He says they do clients a disservice: clients who have goals but no clear idea how to reach them are still "at sea".
sections.simple: Strategies are the actions that get clients to their goals. Finding several possible routes frees clients who feel stuck and boosts their self-efficacy. Helpers should not skip this step as too mechanical, because clients with goals but no means are still lost.
keyPoints: Strategies are actions that help clients accomplish goals; linked to the bias-toward-action value (Chapter 2).
Developing a range of strategies is an exercise in liberation and builds self-efficacy.
Strategy is the art of choosing realistic courses of action under adverse conditions, such as war.
Clients' problem situations are adverse conditions; clients are often at war with themselves and their world.
Skipping this step because it seems mechanical leaves clients 'at sea'.

sections.heading: Principles for Discovering Viable Strategies: Use Brainstorming to Stimulate Clients' Thinking
sections.detailed:
The general principle. Helping clients find strategies once again means stimulating their imagination and encouraging divergent thinking. Most clients do not naturally look for several routes to a goal and then pick the most sensible. The principles here resemble those used in Stage II to find possibilities for a better future.

Brainstorming. Brainstorming, introduced in Chapter 11, is valuable for developing strategies because people usually decide better when they can choose among several options. As in Stage II, brainstorming in Stage III must be focused.

Mara's brainstorm. Mara's first goal is a social life beyond home and work. She asks for two weeks, carries a notepad and records ideas as they come. Her list includes: attending selected alumni events of her local alma mater and volunteering with the alumni association; joining LinkedIn, Facebook and more specialised networking sites; trying a nondenominational church group; starting a part-time MBA to meet people with similar business aims; a two-week volunteer stint at a Georgia camp helping Iranian-American youth with cross-cultural issues; two more weeks in Iran to clarify what she means by "community"; checking the social activities of Iranian Alliances Across Borders; looking for online Iranian networking sites and trying some online "friendships"; volunteering at a local hospital; investigating civic clubs, single women's clubs and women's book clubs; and accepting colleagues' invitations to dinner.

Action can begin early. Mara acted on some ideas immediately: she joined LinkedIn, interviewed the head of alumni relations and attended an alumni event, and arranged a short visit to the Georgia camp to explore a summer internship as some kind of counsellor. Egan stresses that work at any stage can trigger small actions that keep clients moving in the right direction.

Prompt and fade. Helpers may offer suggestions, but the client must stay in the driver's seat; therapists do not make choices for clients directly or indirectly but help them make life-enhancing decisions. In the "prompt and fade" technique the counsellor offers a couple of possibilities, or mentions what others in similar situations have tried, and invites the client to consider them or use them to spark ideas. The "fade" part keeps it from becoming advice-giving: it remains clear that the client must think the options through, choose and commit.

The case of Elton. Elton, a counselling psychology graduate student, is a perfectionist who agonises over what he could have done better; fellow trainees say his "edge" makes them uncomfortable and disrupts the helping flow. He realises that "less is more" and sets the goal of being more relaxed in sessions, freeing himself from the imperative to be perfect, and learning from mistakes rather than spending excessive effort avoiding them. In dialogue with his supervisor he generates strategies:
- Shift his attention from himself to the client and the client's goals.
- Drop inhibiting beliefs: that technical perfection in the model matters more than the relationship ("rehumanising" helping), and that he must be best in the class (the academic-game mentality; practice sessions are real life, not a game).
- Do a 5–10 minute "mini-prep" before each session, as his peers Jerry and Philomena do, reviewing where the client is and how to add value next time.
- When debriefing weekly training videos, start with what is happening with the client rather than his own behaviour.
- Share the discussion with his training partner.
- Put his perfectionism on the agenda of his weekly lifestyle group, which he had avoided because he wanted to be seen as competent.

Egan notes that the supervisor's empathy, probes and invitations to self-challenge produced several strategies for developing a more client-focused mentality.
sections.simple: Like Stage II, finding strategies means encouraging clients to think creatively and generate many options; brainstorming should be focused. Mara listed many ways to build a social life and acted on some at once. Helpers can suggest options using 'prompt and fade' so the client still decides. Elton's supervisor helped him generate strategies to overcome perfectionism.
keyPoints: Help clients use divergent thinking; most do not naturally look for multiple routes to a goal.
Brainstorming (Chapter 11) helps because people decide better with several options; it must be focused.
Mara's two-week brainstorm produced a long list and immediate small actions (LinkedIn, alumni event, Georgia camp visit).
'Prompt and fade': helper offers possibilities, then fades so the client chooses and commits; avoids advice-giving.
Elton's supervisor used empathy, probes and invitations to self-challenge to help him find strategies against perfectionism.

sections.heading: Use Frameworks for Stimulating Clients' Thinking About Strategies
sections.detailed:
Simple frameworks. Helpers can use simple frameworks to frame questions and probes that help clients generate a range of strategies. The framework Egan offers directs clients to the resources in their lives: individuals, models, communities, places, things, organisations, programmes and personal resources.

The case of Jackson. Jackson has terminal cancer and probably less than a year to live. He wants the year to be as full as possible yet realistic. He hates hospitals, especially large anonymous ones; his goals are to die outside hospital, as peacefully as possible, keeping his faculties as long as he can. The framework helps him find strategies:

- Individuals: Who might help? He finds a local doctor who specialises in chronic cancer pain and teaches pain-management techniques; he thinks his wife and daughter could learn to give simple injections; a friend's father received excellent hospice care and died at home; and he plans occasional talks with a respected friend whose wife died of cancer, to find courage.
- Models and exemplars: Who is already doing what the client wants? A co-worker died of cancer at home; Jackson visited him and got the idea of dying outside hospital. The friend refused "poor-me" talk and saw dying as part of living, a model of upbeat attitudes.
- Communities: Through which communities might strategies be found? His parish, though he is not a regular churchgoer, turns out to have a sophisticated approach to services for the sick; an Internet search reveals self-help groups for people like him.
- Places: Are there places that might help? He thinks of a pilgrimage to Lourdes, not expecting miracles but hoping to experience life more deeply, and he has the time and money. He also finds a "high-tech place", an Internet chat room for cancer patients and caregivers, where he can sometimes be a helper rather than a client.
- Things: What things can help? He reads about drug combinations to stave off pain and chemotherapy side effects and about electrical stimulation for chronic pain, explores them with his doctor and seeks second opinions.
- Organisations: He finds an Internet-based organisation offering social support to cancer patients and volunteers; as a helper he gets as much help, motivation and solace as he gives. Mara, too, explores Iranian Alliances Across Borders and PARSA, whose website describes aims of preserving Persian arts and culture, developing leaders through fellowships and awards, and encouraging civic engagement.
- Programmes: Are there ready-made programmes for people in the client's position? A new hospice nearby offers three: one helps the terminally ill stay in the community as long as possible, one provides for part-time residents, and one is residential for those who can spend little or no time in the community. Their goals are practically the same as Jackson's.

Box 13.1: questions for developing strategies. Helpers can help clients ask themselves: Now that I know what I want, what must I do? What are the different routes to my destination? What actions will get me there? What must I do to bridge the gaps between what I have and what I want and need? How many ways are there to reach my goals? How do I get started? What can I do right away? What do I need to do later?
sections.simple: Helpers can use a simple checklist of resources (people, models, communities, places, things, organisations, programmes) to prompt clients to think of strategies. Jackson, who is dying of cancer and wants to die outside hospital, found strategies in each category. Box 13.1 lists questions clients can ask themselves to find routes to their goals.
keyPoints: Frameworks help helpers formulate probes about resources: individuals, models, communities, places, things, organisations, programmes, personal resources.
Jackson (terminal cancer) wanted to die outside hospital, peacefully and with his faculties intact.
Each category yielded strategies: pain doctor, a co-worker as model, parish services, Lourdes and a chat room, pain drugs, a support organisation, hospice programmes.
Helping others (volunteering) gave Jackson as much as he gave.
Box 13.1 lists questions such as 'What are the different routes?' and 'What can I do right away?'

sections.heading: Help Clients Determine the Kind of Working Knowledge and Skills They Will Need to Move Forward
sections.detailed:
Skills deficits. People often get into trouble, or fail to get out of it, because they lack the life skills or coping skills that their problem situations demand. In such cases, helping clients find ways to learn the skills they need is an important broad strategy. Egan cites Carkhuff's (1971) phrase "training as treatment": skills training as part of therapy may be essential for some clients. Pushing clients into activities for which they lack the skills compounds the problem rather than solving it. So the helper asks what working knowledge and skills the client needs to reach the goal.

The case of Jerzy and Zelda. After about two fairly trouble-free years of marriage, the problems of living closely together surfaced. They had relied on romantic fervour to overcome, or more often ignore, difficulties; once it cooled they fought about finances, sex and values. They lacked key interpersonal communication skills. Their nine-year age gap became a problem because neither understood the other's developmental needs: Jerzy knew little about the developmental demands of a 20-year-old woman, and Zelda knew little about the cultural blueprints shaping her 29-year-old husband's lifestyle. Having few problem-solving skills, they could not handle the situation. They needed both working knowledge and skills; Egan notes that lack of interpersonal communication and other life skills is often at the heart of relationship breakdown.

A marriage counsellor's group programme. Egan describes a counsellor who works with groups of four couples and builds communication training into the process. He separates men and women and trains them in tuning in, active listening and responding with empathy. For practice he first pairs women with women and men with men, then men with women who are not their spouses, and finally spouses with each other. Spouses are then taught a simple version of the problem-management process and helped to use their new skills to solve problems together. In this way he equips them with two sets of life skills, interpersonal communication and problem solving, which is his way of pursuing the second goal of helping described in Chapter 1.
sections.simple: Many clients struggle because they lack the skills or knowledge their situation needs, so teaching skills can itself be a strategy (Carkhuff's 'training as treatment'). Jerzy and Zelda's marriage suffered from poor communication and little understanding of each other's developmental needs. One counsellor trains couples in groups in communication and then problem-solving.
keyPoints: Lack of life or coping skills often causes or maintains problems; skills training is an important broad strategy.
Carkhuff (1971) called skills training within therapy 'training as treatment'.
Asking clients to act without the needed skills compounds the problem.
Jerzy and Zelda lacked communication skills, developmental understanding and problem-solving skills.
A counsellor trains groups of four couples in communication, then problem solving, in staged pairings (second goal of helping, Chapter 1).

sections.heading: Task III-B: Help Clients Choose Best-Fit Strategies
sections.detailed:
Decision-making mode again. In Task III-B, clients are once more making decisions, with all the pitfalls and promise that involves. After brainstorming, they need to choose a single strategy or a "package" of strategies that best fits their situation, resources, personality and preferences, and then turn it into some kind of plan for constructive change.

Formality is not the point. Egan says it does not matter whether these tasks are done with the formality the book outlines. Counsellors who understand what planning is and what makes it work can add value by helping clients reach their goals in a systematic, flexible, personalised and cost-effective way.

Why the task is needed. Once they have a range of strategies, some clients move ahead on their own, choosing the best ones, forming a plan and implementing it. Others need help choosing what fits, so Task III-B is added to the process. Brainstorming is useless if clients do not know what to do with the strategies it produces.
sections.simple: After generating options, clients must pick the strategy or package of strategies that best suits their situation, resources, personality and preferences. Some clients do this alone, but others need help. Brainstorming is pointless if clients can't choose among the results.
keyPoints: Clients choose a strategy or 'package' of strategies fitting situation, resources, personality and preferences.
Formality is not the point; help should be systematic, flexible, personalised and cost-effective.
Some clients choose and plan on their own; others need help.
Brainstorming is useless if clients do not know what to do with the strategies generated.

sections.heading: Bud's Amazing Odyssey
sections.detailed:
Background. Bud was helped to find two best-fit strategies for emotional stability, and the results surpassed all expectations. At 18 he woke one morning unable to speak or move; he was hospitalised and diagnosed with catatonic schizophrenia. After repeated admissions with drug treatment and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), the diagnosis became paranoid schizophrenia and he was considered incurable.

Unmanaged life problems. His early history suggests much of his distress came from unmanaged problems and lack of human support. He was separated from his mother for four years as a child; when reunited they moved to a city new to both, where he was harassed at school for his "ethnic" looks and accent. Too much stress and change led him to withdraw, flooded with loss, fear, rage and abandonment, until even small changes were intolerable. His catatonic attack came on the autumn day clocks changed from daylight saving to standard time, an ordinary change that seemed to be the last straw.

Turning point. In hospital Bud became convinced that he and other patients could do something about their illnesses rather than be victims of their own helplessness or of institutions. He later said the "help" (drugs and ECT) was so debilitating it was no wonder he got crazier. Using his own inner resources he got out, found a job and a partner, and married. Later, after family and work problems, he became agitated, felt he was choking and was sent back to hospital. There he met Sandra, a psychiatric social worker who believed many patients were there because of lack of support before, during and after illness. She helped him see his need for social support, especially under stress, and noticed in her inpatient groups that he had a knack for helping others.

Goals and strategies. Bud's broad goal remained emotional stability. Finding support and helping others cope, which were instrumental goals, became his best strategies for achieving it. After discharge he enlisted Sandra to coach his wife on supporting him under stress, then started a self-help group for ex-patients, in which he was a full participant. Because he also wanted to help others like himself, he developed it into a network of self-help groups.

Egan's lesson. Bud focused on one broad goal, translated it into immediate practical goals, discovered two broad strategies (ongoing emotional support and helping others), turned them into practical applications and so achieved stability. His case is not the norm, but it shows the power of problem management combined with a clear sense of self-responsibility.
sections.simple: Bud, diagnosed with schizophrenia and called incurable, found two best-fit strategies for emotional stability: getting social support and helping others. With social worker Sandra's help he had his wife coached to support him, started a self-help group for ex-patients, and grew it into a network. His case shows the power of problem management plus self-responsibility.
keyPoints: Bud was diagnosed with catatonic, then paranoid, schizophrenia and judged incurable after drugs and ECT.
His distress stemmed largely from unmanaged life problems and lack of support; a clock change was 'the last straw'.
Sandra, a psychiatric social worker, showed him his need for support and his knack for helping others.
Two broad strategies (instrumental goals): finding support and helping others, serving the broad goal of emotional stability.
He started a self-help group and then a network of groups; not the norm, but shows problem management plus self-responsibility.

sections.heading: Criteria for Choosing Goal-Accomplishing Strategies: Specific and Effective Strategies
sections.detailed:
The criteria. The criteria for choosing strategies mirror those for choosing goals in Stage II. Strategies, like goals, should be specific, robust, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective and in keeping with the client's values. Clients need not know the full list, though it may help, but the helper must. Egan illustrates several criteria with cases.

Specific strategies. Strategies should be specific enough to drive behaviour. Bud's two broad strategies, tapping into human support and helping others, became concrete ones: keeping in touch with Sandra, getting help from his wife, joining a self-help group, starting one, and founding and running a self-help organisation.

The contrast: Stacy. Stacy was admitted to a mental hospital after bizarre behaviour: dressing in a slovenly way and admonishing neighbours for their "sins". She was diagnosed with schizophrenia, simple type, and had lived alone, increasingly alienated, for about five years since her husband died. Medication controlled some symptoms: she stopped admonishing people and cared for herself, but stayed withdrawn and moderately depressed. She was assigned to "milieu" therapy, which Egan calls a euphemism for following the hospital's general routine (some work, some exercise, some programmed socialising). No therapeutic goals were set and the non-specific programme was totally inadequate. Milieu therapy failed because it was not specific to her needs; it was only marginally better than drug-focused standard care. Bud's strategies, by contrast, gave him stability and a new perspective on life.

Effective strategies. Strategies are effective to the extent that, when implemented, they actually achieve the goal. They may be big, like Bud's, or small, as in Stacy's programme. Stacy's original strategies were too general and lacked bite; Bud's self-chosen ones were big and effective, especially starting and running a self-help organisation.

What worked for Stacy. A newly hired psychiatrist saw she needed more than standard or milieu care and placed her in a comprehensive social-learning programme including cognitive restructuring, social-skills training and behavioural-change interventions based on incentives, shaping, modelling and rewards. Despite ups and downs she responded very well, was discharged within six months and, with an outpatient extension of the programme, stayed in the community.

Meeting all the criteria. For Stacy the new programme was specific, effective, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective and value-consistent. It was cost-effective in two ways: it was the best use of her time, energy and psychological resources, and it helped her and others like her return to and stay in the community. It fitted her values because, though some staff thought she only wanted to be left alone, deep down she valued companionship and freedom, and she did better in the community.
sections.simple: Strategies should meet the same criteria as goals: specific, robust, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective and value-consistent. Specific strategies drive behaviour, as Bud's did, while Stacy's vague 'milieu therapy' achieved nothing. Effective strategies actually reach the goal; Stacy improved only when given a targeted social-learning programme.
keyPoints: Strategies, like goals, should be specific, robust, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective and value-consistent.
The helper must know the criteria even if the client does not.
Specific: strategies must drive behaviour; Bud's broad strategies became concrete actions.
Stacy's non-specific milieu therapy, with no goals set, was totally inadequate.
Effective: strategies must actually achieve the goal; a social-learning programme got Stacy discharged within six months.
Stacy's new programme was cost-effective in two ways and fitted her real values (companionship, freedom).

sections.heading: Realistic Strategies
sections.detailed:
Definition. Clients who choose strategies beyond their resources are "doing themselves in". Strategies are realistic when they can be carried out with the client's resources, are under the client's control, and are free of obstacles.

Do not underestimate clients. Bud's strategies would have looked unrealistic to most clients and helpers. Just as helpers should invite clients to consider stretch goals, they should not underestimate what actions clients can take to move beyond their problems.

The case of Desmond. Desmond lived in a halfway house after leaving a state mental hospital and still had occasional incapacitating bouts of depression. He wanted a job to feel better about himself, become more independent and manage his depression. He applied randomly and was repeatedly rejected after interviews; he lacked the resources to present himself well and was not ready for a regular full-time job. On his own he chose poor strategies even for modest goals.

What changed. A local university received funds for outreach to halfway houses, including finding companies willing to work with residents on a win-win basis. A programme counsellor put Desmond in touch with companies that had specific programmes for people with psychiatric problems; some of their best workers had disabilities, including psychiatric ones. After a few interviews he got a job in one company suited to his situation and capabilities, with a work culture designed to provide the support he needed.

Realism versus selling short. Egan adds that realism is not the same as letting clients sell themselves short. Substantive strategies that make clients stretch for a valued goal can be very rewarding, and Bud's case is an exceptional example.
sections.simple: Realistic strategies fit the client's resources, are under their control and are not blocked by obstacles. Desmond kept failing job interviews until a university outreach programme linked him with supportive companies. But helpers should not let clients sell themselves short; stretching can pay off, as Bud showed.
keyPoints: Realistic strategies: within the client's resources, under the client's control, unencumbered by obstacles.
Strategies beyond a client's resources mean clients are 'doing themselves in'.
Do not underestimate what clients can do; Bud's strategies looked unrealistic to most.
Desmond moved from random job applications to a supportive company via a university outreach programme.
Realism differs from selling oneself short; stretch strategies can be rewarding.

sections.heading: Strategies in Keeping with the Client's Values
sections.detailed:
The principle. Helpers should make sure the strategies chosen are consistent with the client's values.

The priest's case. Egan returns to the priest unjustly accused of child molestation. Preparing for trial, his lawyer wanted to destroy the accusers' credibility and had dug up "dirt" from their pasts. The priest objected that using such tactics would bring him down to their level. He discussed the matter with his counsellor, his superiors and another lawyer, held his ground, and built as strong a case as possible on facts alone, without sleaze. After his acquittal he said this was one of the hardest issues he faced: part of him felt that, being innocent, any means were permitted; another part said this was wrong. The counsellor helped him clarify and challenge his values but did not try to impose his own or the lawyer's values.

Mara and value-consistent strategies. Mara wonders which package of strategies offers the best route into community. She notices how many involve reconnecting with her Iranian roots and wonders if this is her way of moving away from her cultural "neutrality"; she realises some of her depressive feelings come from feeling "bland", and her Iranian roots seem to offer more colour than mainstream American culture. This sparks a new idea: living for a while with an American family, perhaps a lively extended family with more "noble" values than those driving her cousins, perhaps Asian or Hispanic rather than traditional white American.

Box 13.2: questions on best-fit strategies. Clients can ask: Which strategies will be most useful in getting what I need and want? Which are best for this situation? Which best fit my resources? Which are most economical in the use of resources? Which are most powerful? Which best fit my preferred way of acting? Which best fit my values? Which will have the fewest unwanted consequences?
sections.simple: Chosen strategies must fit the client's values. A priest falsely accused refused his lawyer's plan to smear the accusers and won on facts alone; his counsellor helped him clarify his values without imposing any. Mara realises her strategies reflect a wish to reconnect with her roots. Box 13.2 lists questions for choosing best-fit strategies.
keyPoints: Strategies must be consistent with the client's values.
The priest rejected 'dirt'-digging tactics and was acquitted on a fact-based case.
The counsellor helped him clarify and challenge his values without imposing his own or the lawyer's.
Mara sees her strategies pull toward her Iranian roots and considers living with a lively American family.
Box 13.2: questions on usefulness, resources, economy, power, preferred style, values and fewest unwanted consequences.

sections.heading: Sample, Then Choose
sections.detailed:
The idea. Some clients find it easier to choose a strategy after sampling some of the possibilities.

The business partners. Two partners were in conflict over ownership of the firm's assets. They wanted justice, to preserve the business and, if possible, their relationship. A colleague guided them through samples: they discussed with a lawyer what taking the dispute to court would involve, met a consultant-counsellor specialising in such disputes, and visited an arbitration firm. Sampling had the added benefit of giving their emotions time to cool, and they chose the consultant-counsellor route.

A caution. Some clients might use strategy sampling to put off action. That was not true of Bud: attending a self-help group after leaving hospital was a form of sampling. Impressed as he was, he concluded he could start a group limited to ex-patients that focused more directly on their issues. Mara, too, moved instinctively into strategy sampling after brainstorming and found she was far more ready to explore than she had imagined.
sections.simple: Trying out a few options before committing can make choosing easier. Two feuding business partners sampled court, a consultant-counsellor and arbitration, cooled down, and chose the counsellor. Sampling can be misused to delay action, but Bud and Mara used it productively.
keyPoints: Sampling some possibilities can make choosing strategies easier.
Business partners sampled a lawyer, a consultant-counsellor and an arbitration firm, then chose the consultant-counsellor.
Sampling also gave time for emotions to simmer down.
Risk: some clients use sampling to put off action.
Bud's attending a self-help group was strategy sampling; Mara sampled instinctively after brainstorming.

sections.heading: A Balance-Sheet Method for Choosing Strategies
sections.detailed:
What it is. Balance sheets generally deal with the economics of an enterprise. In therapy, the balance-sheet method helps clients come to grips with the economics of problem management and opportunity development. It can be used for any key decision in helping: whether to seek help, which problem to work on, or which goal to choose. Balance sheets consider the acceptability and unacceptability of both benefits and costs.

The questions. Applied to choosing strategies, the balance sheet asks:
- What are the benefits of this strategy, for me and for significant others?
- To what degree are these benefits acceptable, to me and to significant others?
- In what ways are these benefits unacceptable, to me and to significant others?
- What are the costs of this strategy, for me and for significant others?
- To what degree are these costs acceptable, to me and to significant others?
- In what ways are these costs unacceptable, to me and to significant others?

So the grid crosses benefits and costs, acceptable and unacceptable aspects, and self and significant others. It can be used whenever clients face an important decision, such as setting a goal.

The case of Karen. Karen is married with three teenagers and works in a retailer's accounting department. She finally admits she is an alcoholic because it has become nearly impossible to hide. After several failed attempts to just stop, she admits she does not know how and seeks help. One option is a one-month residential programme at a treatment centre with a high success rate. It appeals to her, but she wonders if it is self-indulgent. Because it is a serious decision, her counsellor Joan helps her use the balance sheet. The programme is costly and will affect her husband, children, workplace and herself ("What will people think of me? What if I fail?"). After completing a version of the balance sheet and discussing it, Karen concludes the residential programme is a good idea, more substantial than outpatient treatment; she is scared but thinks it will help her most. Joan then helps her plan ways to address the pain she is causing her family and workplace.

How to use it. Egan urges a practical, flexible approach. Do not use the balance sheet with every client for every course of action; use it when client and helper think it will help, and tailor it to the client. One of the best ways to use it is not to use it directly at all: keep it in the back of your mind whenever clients make decisions, use it as a filter for listening, and turn relevant parts into probes that help clients see what they may be overlooking. Examples: "How do you think this decision will affect your husband?" or, for an overly optimistic client, "Is there any downside to that strategy?" There is no formula.
sections.simple: The balance sheet helps clients weigh the benefits and costs of a strategy, for themselves and for significant others, and how acceptable or unacceptable each is. Karen used it to decide on a residential alcohol programme. Egan advises using it flexibly, often just as a mental filter that suggests useful probes, not as a formula for every client.
keyPoints: The balance sheet applies the 'economics' of decisions to problem management; usable for any key decision.
It weighs benefits and costs, their acceptability and unacceptability, for self and significant others (six questions).
Karen, an alcoholic, used it with counsellor Joan and chose a one-month residential programme.
Use it practically and flexibly, not with every client or every decision; tailor it.
Best use: keep it in mind as a listening filter and turn parts into probes; 'No formula.'

sections.heading: Help Clients Link Best-Fit Strategies to Action
sections.detailed:
The problem. Some clients are full of great ideas for getting things done but never act. They lack the discipline to evaluate ideas, choose the best and turn them into action, finding such work tedious even though it is exactly what they need.

The case of Clint. Clint learns from his doctor that he is at high risk of heart disease and must change his lifestyle. He is cynical, quick to anger and slow to trust; venting suspicion and hostility only intensifies them. A key change, then, is to alter this pattern and learn to trust. He sets three broad goals: reduce mistrust of others' motives; reduce the frequency and intensity of rage, anger and irritation; and learn to treat others with consideration.

Common strategies (Williams, 1989). Clint reads a list of common strategies for these goals: keeping a hostility log to discover patterns of cynicism and irritation; finding someone trustworthy to talk to; "thought stopping", catching oneself indulging in hostile thoughts or thoughts leading to hostile feelings; talking sense to oneself when tempted to put others down; developing empathic thought patterns (walking in the other's shoes); learning to laugh at one's own silliness; using relaxation techniques, especially to counter negative thoughts; finding ways to practise trust; developing active listening; behaving assertively rather than aggressively; putting things in context, for example seeing each day as one's last or comparing one's problems with those of people with real life-limiting problems; and practising forgiveness without being patronising or condescending.

Clint's experiment. Proud of his rationality (which itself helped get him into trouble), Clint picks strategies that form an "experiment": seeing a counsellor (for objectivity), keeping a hostility log (data gathering), and using thought stopping and self-talk when people get under his skin. The counsellor privately notes that none of these necessarily changes Clint's attitudes toward others, but he does not invite Clint to challenge himself yet. He bets that through "strategy sampling" Clint will learn more about his problem and discover it runs deeper than he thinks. Clint sets about the experiment with vigour.

The lesson. Clint chose strategies that fitted his values, though those values themselves needed review. But he acted, and action gave him the opportunity to learn.
sections.simple: Some clients have plenty of ideas but never act on them. Clint, at risk of heart disease from hostility and mistrust, chose a few strategies from a list (counsellor, hostility log, thought stopping, self-talk) as an 'experiment'. His choices were limited, but acting on them gave him a chance to learn.
keyPoints: Some clients generate ideas but lack discipline to choose and act on them.
Clint's three goals: reduce mistrust, reduce rage/anger/irritation, treat others with consideration.
Common strategies from Williams (1989) include a hostility log, thought stopping, empathic thinking, relaxation, assertiveness and forgiveness.
Clint chose a counsellor, a hostility log, thought stopping and talking sense to himself as an 'experiment'.
The counsellor relied on strategy sampling rather than early challenge; action gave Clint the chance to learn.

sections.heading: The Shadow Side of Selecting Strategies: Three Pitfalls
sections.detailed:
Decision-making pitfalls. The shadow side of decision making operates when clients choose strategies. Egan cites Goslin (1985), whose early description of decision-making pitfalls has since been shown by research (Chapter 1) to be all too common. According to Goslin, when defining a problem people dislike thinking about unpleasant possibilities, find it hard to assign values to alternative actions, tend toward premature closure, overlook or undervalue long-term consequences, and are unduly influenced by the first way a problem is framed. When evaluating consequences they give extra weight to risks that can be known with certainty, are more open to manipulation when their own values are poorly thought out, and struggle to know when to search for more information. In choosing a course of action, clients often fail to evaluate the risks and whether they are balanced by the probability of success.

Three pitfalls. Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey (1972) described three ways clients may handle risk and probability: wishful thinking, playing it safe, and avoiding the worst outcome. Clients often slip into these without reflecting on them or on their unintended downsides, which is why they lie "in the shadows".

1. Wishful thinking. The client chooses a course of action that might, they hope, achieve the goal, regardless of risk, cost or probability. Jenny wants her ex-husband to pay more child support and nags him and tries to make him feel guilty. She ignores the risk (he might get angry and pay nothing), the cost (time and emotional energy spent arguing) and the probability of success (he responds badly to nagging). Wishful thinkers operate blindly, without weighing usefulness; at worst this is reckless. Clients who "work hard" yet "get nowhere" may be persisting with preferred but doubtful means. Effective helpers challenge this, for example by inviting Jenny to review what she has been doing to get Tom to pay and how well it has worked.

2. Playing it safe. The client chooses only low-risk actions with a high probability of at least limited success. Liam, a manager in his early 40s, is unhappy with how his boss treats him: his ideas are ignored, his delegated authority is pre-empted, and his boss will not discuss his career. His instrumental goals are to tell his boss of his dissatisfaction and learn what the boss thinks of him and his prospects; the overall goal is a more promising career path. But he avoids raising issues when the boss is "out of sorts" and does not want to "upset the applecart" when things go well. He drops hints, jokes, tells others hoping word filters back, and lets himself be intimidated in formal appraisals, all while believing he is doing what a "reasonable" man would. He does not see how safe he is playing it.

3. Avoiding the worst outcome. Clients choose means likely to avoid the worst possible result, minimising the maximum danger, often without naming the danger. Crissy, unhappy in her marriage, sets a goal to be "more assertive", but her unspoken maximum danger is losing her partner. So her "assertiveness" is her usual compliance with frills, such as occasionally going out with friends and missing supper, breaks her husband actually enjoys. She never sits down to review the relationship because that might be the beginning of the end. Her counsellor asks how she would react if a good friend told her that Bill has her just where he wants her; startled, Crissy leaves with a more realistic view of what her strategy is, and is not, achieving.
sections.simple: Clients' strategy choices are distorted by common decision-making biases (Goslin): avoiding unpleasant thoughts, closing too early, ignoring long-term consequences, and so on. Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey name three pitfalls: wishful thinking (ignoring risk, cost and odds, like Jenny), playing it safe (Liam), and avoiding the worst outcome (Crissy). Helpers need to challenge these.
keyPoints: Goslin (1985): people avoid unpleasant eventualities, close prematurely, undervalue long-range consequences and are swayed by first formulations.
Clients often fail to weigh risk against probability of success.
Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey (1972): wishful thinking, playing it safe, avoiding the worst outcome.
Wishful thinking ignores risk, cost and probability (Jenny nagging her ex-husband).
Playing it safe chooses low-risk, limited-success actions (Liam with his boss).
Avoiding the worst outcome minimises the maximum danger, often unnamed (Crissy's 'assertiveness').

sections.heading: Striking a Balance
sections.detailed:
The combination approach. According to Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey, in the ideal case clients choose strategies that balance risks against the probability of success. This "combination" approach is the hardest to apply.

What it requires. It involves the right kind of analysis of problem situations and opportunities, choosing goals with the right edge, being clear about one's values, ranking a variety of strategies according to those values, and estimating how effective any given course of action might be. Even more, it requires challenging the blind spots that could distort all these activities.

The helper's role. Egan points out that these are exactly the problem-management tasks helpers should be ready to help clients carry out, at least with clients who are capable of it.
sections.simple: The ideal is to balance risk against the chance of success. This 'combination' approach is the hardest, since it needs good analysis, well-chosen goals, clear values, ranked strategies, realistic estimates and challenging blind spots. Helpers should help capable clients do this.
keyPoints: Ideal: strategies that balance risks against probability of success (the 'combination' approach).
It is the most difficult approach to apply.
Requires sound analysis, goals with the right edge, clear values, ranking strategies by values, and estimating effectiveness.
Also requires challenging blind spots that distort these activities.
These are problem-management tasks helpers should help capable clients perform.

sections.heading: Task III-C: Help Clients Formulate Viable Plans; The Case of Frank: No Plan of Action
sections.detailed:
The logic. After identifying and choosing strategies, clients need to organise them into a plan. In Task III-C counsellors help clients come up with the plan itself: the sequence of actions (what first, what second, and so on) that turns a goal into an outcome. Egan cautions that in practice these tasks, like all tasks of problem management, are often much messier. Therapists need to know where clients are in the "geography" of helping and what they are struggling with in order to know how to intervene.

No plan of action. Lacking a plan, a clear step-by-step process to reach a goal, keeps some clients stuck. Frank, a vice president of a large West Coast corporation, was a business-astute go-getter and heir apparent to Vince, the retiring president. But Vince was a leader, not just a manager: he had a 5–10 year vision, used the Internet early for competitive edge, and related well to people, whom he saw as the company's human capital. He had taken to heart a millennium survey of about two million US employees, whose summary said people join companies but leave supervisors; in the "war for talent" he could not afford alienating supervisors.

Frank's style. Frank was a "hands-on" manager: slow to delegate, second-guessing and reversing others' decisions in ways that put them down, a poor listener and short-term in outlook ("What were last week's figures like?"). He was an operations man, called a micromanager by his direct reports. Vince told him he was a potential successor but that the job demanded a leader, and explained what had to change.

The coaching. Frank began seeing a coach, Roseanne, a former executive in the same industry now consulting for family reasons; he chose her because he trusted her business acumen. They worked for over a year, often in hurried meetings. Frank aimed to become president and, being bright, came up with inventive strategies, but he could never be pinned down to an overall programme with specific milestones. He said he was "too busy" or that a formal programme was "too stifling", oddly, since formal planning was one of his business strengths. He merely dabbled, and after two years Vince appointed someone else. Frank then left the company.

Why it failed. Frank had two blind spots the consultant did not help him overcome. First, he never took Vince's notion of leadership seriously, so he was not ready for a change programme and believed business acumen would win out. Second, he thought he could change his style at the margins when substantial change was needed. Roseanne never challenged him as he kept "trying things" that led nowhere. Egan suggests she might have told him bluntly that he did not buy Vince's idea of leadership, that lip service would not work, and that they should either do something or stop meeting. Frank might then have sought another consultant. In a way she was a co-conspirator, since she too relished their business discussions; she was left to reflect on her success as a consultant and her failure as a coach.
sections.simple: Task III-C turns chosen strategies into a step-by-step plan, though real helping is messier. Frank, a vice president who needed to become a leader to succeed his boss, tried various strategies but never committed to a structured plan with milestones, and lost the presidency. His coach Roseanne failed to challenge his blind spots.
keyPoints: Task III-C organises chosen strategies into a sequence of actions that turns a goal into an outcome.
In practice the process is messy; therapists must know where clients are in the 'geography' of helping.
Frank, a micromanaging vice president, needed to become a leader to succeed Vince.
Frank dabbled in strategies but avoided a programme with milestones and lost the job after two years.
Two blind spots: he did not take Vince's idea of leadership seriously, and he thought marginal change would do.
Coach Roseanne never challenged him; Egan calls her a co-conspirator.

sections.heading: How Plans Add Value to Clients' Change Programs
sections.detailed:
Why review the benefits. Some clients, once they know what they want and some of what they must do, develop a plan and move forward on their own; others need help. Because some clients and helpers fail to appreciate the power of a plan, Egan reviews the advantages of planning.

Little plans. Not all plans are formal. "Little plans" are made and carried out throughout helping. Tess, an alcoholic who wants to stop drinking, needs support; she contacts Lou, a friend who has kicked a drug habit, explains her situation and enlists his help, which he gives. Objective accomplished. Change programmes are full of setting "little objectives" and executing "little plans" to reach them.

Formal plans. Formal planning usually focuses on the sequence of the "big steps" clients must take, answering "What do I need to do first, second and third?" In its most formal version, a plan takes the strategies, divides them into workable steps, puts the steps in order and assigns a timetable for each. Adapted to the individual client, formal planning has several advantages:

1. Plans help clients develop discipline. Many clients get into trouble because they lack discipline; planning places reasonable demands on them. Desmond benefited greatly from a formal job-seeking programme, and ready-made programmes such as AA's 12 steps are plans that demand or encourage self-discipline.
2. Plans keep clients from being overwhelmed. They make goals seem doable by keeping steps "bite-size". Bud began by joining one self-help group; he did not become a self-help entrepreneur overnight, and the process was messy, two steps forward and one back.
3. Formulating plans helps clients search for better strategies. When Sy Johnson's wife and children, with a counsellor, began planning how to cope with their reactions to his alcoholism, they saw their strategies had been hit-or-miss. With an Al-Anon group they went back to the drawing board; planning would help restore order to the family.
4. Plans let clients evaluate the realism and adequacy of goals. This is the "dialogue" that should occur among the stages. Walter, a middle manager who lost his job and was sued by his former employer, saw while planning that getting his job back and winning a countersuit were unrealistic. His revised goals were getting the employer to withdraw the suit and getting ready for a job search through a self-help group for managers who had lost their jobs.
5. Plans make clients aware of the resources they need. Dora, planning to pull her life together after her younger son disappeared, realised she lacked social support; she had withdrawn from friends and relatives. A goal of finding support to get back into community was added.
6. Formulating plans uncovers unanticipated obstacles. Ernesto, a US soldier who accidentally killed an innocent bystander in Afghanistan, struggled to return to civilian life. Only when he tried out plans to normalise his social life did he see how ashamed he was; he felt so flawed that intimacy was almost impossible. Dealing with his shame became a central part of healing.

Time as an ally. Plans will not solve every problem, but they make time an ally rather than an enemy. Many clients engage in aimless activity; plans help them use time well. Planning also has a hefty shadow side, for which Egan refers readers to Dorner (1996).
sections.simple: Plans can be informal 'little plans' (Tess asking a friend for support) or formal ones that break strategies into ordered, timed steps. Formal plans build discipline, keep steps bite-size, prompt better strategies, test whether goals are realistic, reveal needed resources and uncover hidden obstacles. They help clients use time well, though planning has its own shadow side.
keyPoints: 'Little plans' and 'little objectives' run throughout helping (Tess enlisting Lou).
A formal plan divides strategies into workable steps, orders them and gives each a timetable.
Plans build discipline (Desmond, AA's 12 steps) and prevent overwhelm with bite-size steps (Bud).
Planning prompts better strategies (Johnson family), tests goal realism (Walter) and reveals needed resources (Dora).
Planning uncovers unanticipated obstacles (Ernesto's shame).
Plans make time an ally; planning has a shadow side (Dorner, 1996).

sections.heading: Shaping the Plan: Two Cases
sections.detailed:
Plans need shape. A plan needs "shape" to drive action. A formal plan identifies the activities needed to reach a goal or subgoal, places them in a logical but flexible order, and sets a time frame for each key step. A plan should therefore answer three simple questions:
1. What concrete things must be done to accomplish the goal or subgoal?
2. In what sequence should they be done: what first, second, third?
3. What is the time frame: what today, tomorrow, next month?

Subgoals. When goals are complex or difficult, it helps to set subgoals to move step by step toward the ultimate goal. Once Bud decided to start an organisation of self-help groups for ex-patients, he had several subgoals. His first step was a test group, an instrumental goal that gave him experience for further planning. A later step was establishing a charter; "charter in place" was one subgoal on the way to his main goal.

Simplicity. In general, the simpler the plan the better, but simplicity is not an end in itself. The question is not whether a plan is complicated but whether it is well shaped and designed to produce results. Complicated plans broken into subgoals and the activities to reach them are as achievable as simpler ones, provided the time frame is realistic.

Egan then illustrates shaping with two cases, Harriet and Frank revisited.
sections.simple: A good plan has shape: it lists the concrete actions, puts them in sequence, and sets a time frame. Complex goals should be broken into subgoals, as Bud did with a test group and later a charter. Simpler is usually better, but what matters most is that the plan is well shaped to get results.
keyPoints: A formal plan identifies activities, orders them logically but flexibly, and sets time frames.
Three questions: what concrete things, in what sequence, in what time frame.
Complex goals need subgoals; Bud's test group and 'charter in place' were subgoals.
The simpler the plan the better, but simplicity is not an end in itself.
Complicated plans broken into subgoals are achievable if the time frame is realistic.

sections.heading: The Case of Harriet: The Economics of Planning
sections.detailed:
Harriet's situation. Harriet, an undergraduate at a small state college, wants to become a counsellor. The college has no formal counselling psychology programme, but with an adviser she identifies three useful courses: Social Problem-Solving Skills; Effective Interpersonal Communication Skills; and Developmental Psychology: The Developmental Tasks of Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood.

Poor sequencing. She takes the courses as they come up. Unfortunately Social Problem-Solving Skills comes first; it has plenty of skills practice but assumes competence in interpersonal communication. Too late, she realises she is taking the courses out of optimal order and would gain far more had she taken the communication course first.

The peer-helper programme. Harriet also volunteers in the dormitory peer-helper programme run by the Center for Student Services. Its counsellors select people carefully but offer little training; it is learn-as-you-go. She realises the developmental psychology course would have helped her enormously, helping her understand herself and her peers.

Re-planning. She finally sees she needs a better plan. The next semester she drops out of the peer programme, sits down with one of the Center's psychologists, reviews the school's offerings, decides which courses will help most, and works out their proper sequence. He also suggests a couple of courses at a local community college.

The lesson. Harriet's opportunity-development programme would have been far more efficient had it been better shaped from the start. Sequence matters: a plan is not just a list of the right activities but the right activities in the right order.
sections.simple: Harriet, who wants to become a counsellor, took useful courses in the wrong order, starting with problem-solving before communication skills, and volunteered as a peer helper without the developmental psychology that would have helped. With a psychologist's help she re-planned the right courses in the right sequence. Good shaping from the start would have saved effort.
keyPoints: Harriet chose three relevant courses but took them in the order they happened to come up.
Social Problem-Solving Skills assumed communication skills she had not yet learned.
The peer-helper programme offered little training; developmental psychology would have helped.
She re-planned with a Center psychologist, choosing and sequencing courses (plus community college options).
Lesson: her programme would have been more efficient if better shaped from the start; sequence matters.

sections.heading: The Case of Frank Revisited
sections.detailed:
A second chance. Egan imagines what planning might have done for Frank, who, like Scrooge, gets a second chance. The plan is built around the three shaping questions.

What does Frank need to do? To become a leader, he decides to reset his managerial style by involving subordinates more in decision making. He wants to listen more, set work objectives through dialogue, ask for suggestions and delegate more. He also knows he should coach direct reports according to their individual needs, give feedback on the quality of their work, recognise their contributions, and reward results beyond their objectives.

In what sequence? First, he will call in each subordinate and ask what they need from him to get their job done, how he can add value to their work, and what management style would help them most. That dialogue will help him tailor his supervision to each person. Second, because the business planning cycle is about to begin and each person needs objectives, it is the ideal time to set objectives through dialogue rather than assigning them. He sends a memo asking each direct report to review the company's strategy and business plan and those of their own function, and to write down what their key managerial objectives for the year should be, including "stretch" goals.

What time frame? Frank calls in each subordinate immediately, completes the objective-setting sessions within three weeks, and puts off further action on delegation until he has a better reading of their performance.

The condition. This rough plan might have transformed his chaotic and abortive attempt at change, but only on condition that he was convinced a different approach to management made personal and business sense. A plan cannot substitute for real commitment to the goal.

Box 13.3: questions on planning. Helpers can help clients ask: Which sequence of actions will get me to my goal? Which actions are most critical? How important is their order? What is the best time frame for each? Which step needs substeps? How can I build informality and flexibility into my plan? How do I gather the resources, including social support, needed to implement it?
sections.simple: Egan re-imagines Frank with a proper plan: what to do (listen, set objectives through dialogue, delegate, coach, give feedback), in what order (first ask each subordinate what they need, then set objectives together), and when (immediately, finishing within three weeks, delaying delegation). It would only work if Frank actually believed in the change. Box 13.3 lists planning questions.
keyPoints: Frank 'like Scrooge' gets a second chance in Egan's fantasy.
What: involve subordinates, listen, set objectives through dialogue, delegate, coach, give feedback, recognise and reward.
Sequence: first ask each report what they need; second, set objectives (including stretch goals) through dialogue in the planning cycle.
Time frame: meetings immediately, objective-setting within three weeks, delegation postponed.
Works only if Frank is convinced the new approach makes personal and business sense.
Box 13.3: sequence, critical actions, order, time frame, substeps, flexibility, resources and social support.

sections.heading: Principles for Humanizing the Mechanics of Constructive Change: Build a Planning Mentality into the Helping Process Right from the Start
sections.detailed:
Planning in the real world. Egan recalls lending a friend a detailed self-development book; two weeks later the friend threw it on his desk asking who would go through all that. Egan's retort, that someone really interested in self-development would, was in his own words the righteous rather than the realistic response. Real-world planning seldom looks like textbook planning; textbooks supply useful frameworks and principles, but these are rarely implemented exactly as written. Most people are too impatient for detailed planning. One reason for the dismal record of discretionary change (Chapter 2) is that even clients who set realistic goals lack the discipline to make reasonable plans; the detailed work is too burdensome.

A human face. Stages II and III, with their six tasks, need a human face. Helpers who skip the goal-setting and planning steps clients need shortchange them. But helpers who are pedantic, mechanistic or awkward risk alienating clients, who may feel they are getting "boring garbage". Egan therefore offers principles to guide the constructive-change process.

Principle 1: build a planning mentality in from the start. A constructive-change mind-set should permeate helping from the beginning. Helpers should see clients as self-healing agents able to change their lives, not just people mired in problems. Even while listening to the story, the helper should start thinking how the situation could be remedied and probe what approaches to change the client is considering, however tentative. Helping clients act in their real world from the start builds an initial planning mentality. If helping is to be solution-focused, strategies and plans must be raised early, for example by asking what the client has done so far to cope.

The case of Cora. Cora, a battered wife, did not want to leave her husband because of the children. From the start the helper saw her situation in terms of the whole helping process; while listening without distortion, she saw possible goals and strategies. In sessions Cora learned how battered women typically respond and how dysfunctional some responses are, how to stop blaming herself, and how to overcome fears of more active coping. At home she confronted her husband and stopped submitting to violence in a vain attempt to avoid further abuse. She joined a self-help group for battered women, where she found support and learned to invoke police protection and the courts. Further sessions helped her shift identity from battered woman to survivor to doer, moving from facing problems to developing opportunities.

Not imposed programmes. Such constructive-change scenarios should be in the helper's mind from the start, not as preset programmes to be imposed but as part of a constructive-change mentality.
sections.simple: Real people rarely plan the way textbooks describe, so goal-setting and planning need a human face: skipping them shortchanges clients, but being mechanical alienates them. The first principle is to have a change-and-planning mindset from the very first session, seeing clients as able to heal themselves. Cora, a battered wife, moved from victim to survivor to doer this way.
keyPoints: Real-world planning seldom matches textbook planning; most people find detailed planning too burdensome.
Lack of planning discipline helps explain the dismal record of discretionary change (Chapter 2).
Stages II and III need a human face: neither skip them nor be pedantic and mechanistic.
Principle 1: build a planning mentality in from the start; see clients as self-healing agents.
Ask early, 'What have you done so far to cope?'; Cora moved from battered woman to survivor to doer.
Change scenarios are part of a mentality, not preset programmes imposed on clients.

sections.heading: Adapt the Constructive-Change Process to the Style of the Client
sections.detailed:
Formal or informal. Setting goals, devising strategies and making and implementing plans can be done formally or informally. Kirschenbaum (1985) challenged the idea that a plan must always be an exact blueprint of specific actions, sequence and time frame. He suggested helpers ask: How specific do the activities have to be? How rigid does the order have to be? How soon must each activity be carried out? He argued that in some cases being less specific and rigid about actions, sequencing and deadlines can encourage people to keep choosing their activities flexibly as they pursue goals. Flexibility in planning can make clients more self-reliant and proactive.

A continuum. Some clients actually like detailed planning because it fits their style. Gitta sought counselling as she entered the "empty nest" period; there were no specific problems, but she saw too much emptiness ahead. Her counsellor helped her see this as a normal developmental opportunity and challenge rather than a psychological problem (Raup and Myers, 1989), a chance to reset her life. After discussing maladaptive responses to this transition, they reviewed possible scenarios. Gitta loved brainstorming, detailing scenarios, weighing choices, setting strategies and making formal plans; she had run her household this way for years, so the process was familiar though the content was new.

The skewed distribution. Gitta may be the exception. The distribution is skewed toward the "I hate all this detail and won't do it" end, and rigid planning can lead to frequent failure to reach short-term goals. Yousef, a single parent of a son with intellectual disability (the book's term is "mentally retarded"), was told by a colleague that he had let his son become a ball and chain, which was bad for both. Stung, he reluctantly sought counselling. He never discussed an extensive change programme, but with a little stimulation he started doing small things differently: when he came home tired and frustrated, a friend from his building would drop by, which helped him not take frustrations out on his son; on weekends, instead of staying cooped up, he went to the zoo and art museum with a woman friend and his son, and found his son enjoyed these greatly. He found small ways to blend caring for his son with a better social life. His counsellor had a constructive-change mentality from the start but did not push formal planning.

Avoiding the slipshod. A slipshod approach ("I'll pull myself together one of these days") is also self-defeating, even fatal, as our own experience shows.

The guiding rule. Counsellors should help clients adopt the degree of rigour in planning that makes sense for them. There are no formulas, only client needs, planning skills and common sense. Some things must be done now, some later; some clients need more slack; sometimes actions should be spelled out specifically, at other times only in broad terms, leaving the rest to the client's judgment.

Brief therapy. If therapy is brief, help clients start doing things that lead to their goals; in a later session help them review, drop what is not working, continue what is, add more effective strategies and organise their programme more. With limited sessions, extensive goal setting and planning is impossible; the ongoing challenge in brief therapy is "What can I do that will add most value?"
sections.simple: Planning can be formal or informal, and helpers should match it to the client. Kirschenbaum argued that less rigid plans can make clients more self-reliant. Gitta loved detailed planning, but most people hate it; Yousef improved through small informal changes. Avoid both rigidity and sloppiness, and in brief therapy focus on getting clients doing things and then reviewing them.
keyPoints: Kirschenbaum (1985): ask how specific, how rigid in order, and how soon activities must be.
Less rigid planning can help clients choose activities flexibly and become more self-reliant and proactive.
Gitta (empty nest) enjoyed formal planning; her transition was framed as a developmental opportunity (Raup and Myers, 1989).
Most clients are at the 'I hate all this detail' end; rigid plans can lead to frequent failure of short-term goals.
Yousef made small informal changes; a slipshod approach is also self-defeating.
No formulas: client needs, planning skills and common sense; in brief therapy ask 'What adds most value?'

sections.heading: Outline a Plan for the Client and Then Help the Client Tailor It to His or Her Needs
sections.detailed:
Using experience. As helpers gain experience, they learn more about programme development and what kinds of programmes work for different clients. They build a stockpile of useful programmes and learn to stitch pieces together into new ones. They can use this to fashion a plan for clients who lack the skills or temperament to create one.

Not fostering dependence. The aim is not dependence but growth in self-determination. So helpers can first offer a plan as a sketch or outline rather than a detailed programme, then work with the client to fill it out and adapt it to their needs and style.
