The case of Katrina. Katrina dropped out of high school but earned an equivalency diploma. She was overweight and reclusive and had restricted her activities over the years because of her weight; sporadic diets left her heavier. Chronically depressed and with little imagination, she could not produce a coherent plan. Once her counsellor understood the problem, she pulled together an outline change programme including blame reduction, redefining beauty, decreasing self-imposed social restrictions, and cognitive restructuring to lessen depression. She also supplied information about obesity and suggestions from health-care sources. She presented these simply, adding detail only for clarity, and added more detail as Katrina became involved in planning and making choices.

Freedom to invent. This counsellor drew on existing programmes, but counsellors may also design their own from expertise and experience. The point is to give clients something to work with and get involved in; the plan is elaborated through dialogue and in the amount of detail the client can handle.

The ultimate test. The effectiveness of plans is judged by the problem-managing and opportunity-developing action clients take to get what they need and want. There is no such thing as a good plan in itself. Life-enhancing outcomes, not planning or hard work, are the final arbiter.
sections.simple: Experienced helpers can sketch a plan for clients who cannot make one themselves, then help them fill in and adapt it, so clients grow in self-determination rather than dependence. Katrina's counsellor offered a simple outline and added detail as Katrina got involved. A plan is only as good as the outcomes it produces.
keyPoints: Experienced helpers build a stockpile of programmes and can stitch pieces together.
They can offer a sketch or outline plan to clients lacking the skills or temperament to plan.
The aim is self-determination, not dependence; clients fill out and tailor the outline.
Katrina's outline: blame reduction, redefining beauty, fewer self-imposed restrictions, cognitive restructuring, obesity information.
No plan is good in itself; life-enhancing outcomes are the final arbiter.

sections.heading: Help Clients Develop Contingency Plans
sections.detailed:
Why contingencies. If the future is uncertain, it pays to keep a broad range of options open. There is no point investing heavily in a goal or programme that will have to change because the client's world changes. So helpers should help clients choose one or more backup goals. Clients then have direction and contingency; if circumstances change they can choose the goal that best fits. Choosing a goal or programme is not a once-and-for-all decision: the client sticks with it until it is no longer viable or a better one emerges. Viable options make it easier to drop, or put on the back burner, an option that no longer works. Backup plans give freedom and flexibility and protect clients from the status quo decision-making trap described earlier.

The case of Linda. Linda, born and raised in Iraq, works for a computer firm in Mexico after a tortuous journey through South and Central America as an illegal immigrant, including prostitution and life-threatening experiences. The upside is that she has learned to live by her wits. After an illegal trip to the United States, her one goal is to live there permanently, and she tells a lawyer friend she plans to live there illegally, feeling intelligent and savvy enough to manage it. Knowing her ultimate goal, the lawyer helps her review instrumental goals, goals in themselves but also steps toward the ultimate one: obtaining political refugee status, becoming a green card holder, marrying a US citizen, marrying a foreigner likely to get a green card, or entering the quota of immigrants admitted for essential skills such as those needed in booming technology industries. Each would need its own plan. Her future remains risky and uncertain; she must pick the instrumental goal that offers the best chance, but she now has fall-back options.

Contingency in strategies too. Goals may need changing ("If I don't get into medical school, the nurse-practitioner route is still attractive"), and strategies may need changing too. Contingency plans answer "What will I do if my chosen plan is not working?" and make clients more effective tacticians. We make them because we live in an imperfect world. They are especially needed when clients choose a high-risk programme for a critical goal. Backup plans also build responsibility: if a plan is not working, clients must decide whether to try the alternative. Contingency plans need not be complicated; a counsellor might simply ask, "If that doesn't work, then what will you do?"
sections.simple: Because the future is uncertain, clients should have backup goals and backup plans. This gives direction plus flexibility and stops clients clinging to the status quo. Linda, set on living in the US illegally, was helped to see several legal routes as alternatives. A simple 'If that doesn't work, then what?' can be enough.
keyPoints: Uncertain futures call for backup goals; choosing a goal is not a once-and-forever decision.
Backup plans give freedom and flexibility and help avoid the status quo decision-making trap.
Linda's lawyer friend helped her review instrumental goals: refugee status, green card, marriage, skilled-immigrant quota.
Contingency plans answer 'What will I do if my plan isn't working?' and make clients better tacticians.
Especially needed for high-risk programmes for critical goals; they also build responsibility.
They can be simple: 'If that doesn't work, then what will you do?'

sections.heading: Ready-Made Action Programs; Ready-Made Therapeutic Interventions: Evidence-Supported Treatments (EST)
sections.detailed:
Beyond basic problem management. The book has focused on clients with messy problems in living: helping them explore problem situations, identify desired outcomes, devise action programmes and implement plans. But by some counts there are hundreds of ready-made therapy and well-being programmes that expand and complement basic therapeutic skills. The previous edition discussed some; here Egan only names and briefly describes them, noting that they will be part of the curriculum of any therapist training programme.

Evidence-supported treatments. Researchers and practitioners have designed evidence-based programmes for a wide range of mental health problems. Terminology varies; Egan calls them evidence-supported treatments (ESTs). They are validated by rigorous research and come with step-by-step manuals for training and clinical use. For example, ESTs exist for almost every type of phobia. Egan names David Barlow as a pioneer of evidence-based practice. Many ESTs are simple step-by-step processes that both therapist and client can learn easily, for instance for anxiety, but some are relatively complex.

Barlow's unified protocol. A more complex example is the new step-by-step protocol of Barlow and associates for treating several disorders including depression, anxiety and phobias. Barlow claims it takes three or four basic concepts present in all successful treatments for these emotional disorders and combines them into a single, unified, "transdiagnostic" set of principles clinicians can adapt to any client. Its seven modules are: psychoeducation; motivational enhancement to engage clients in treatment; emotional awareness training, including present-focused awareness; cognitive appraisal and reappraisal; modifying emotion-driven behaviours and emotional avoidance; exposure to actual emotional experience; and relapse prevention. Barlow says it offers more treatment flexibility than most manuals.

The backlash. There has been a backlash against the evidence-based treatment movement, not because ESTs are not useful "in their place", but because of professional disagreement and politics over where that place is and over the nature and scope of the movement. ESTs also tend to deal with isolated symptoms rather than the problems in living clients struggle with. There is no ready-made programme for, say, a distressed couple from two cultural backgrounds, one partner bipolar, disputing finances and how to raise their three children.

Both-and, not either-or. Is it useful to include relevant ESTs in such treatment? Certainly. The choice is not either the common-factors approach or evidence-based practice; a both-and approach based on client needs is called for. Egan's "ingredients of successful therapy" approach does not oppose ESTs: use whatever helps clients manage their problem situations.

Hot debates. The complex debate over ready-made programmes is beyond the book's remit, and the basics it teaches are needed on both sides. Open questions include: What relevance does the medical model have to psychotherapy? Should the emphasis be on the client or the treatment? How far is therapy shaped by economics and third-party payers? How does probability in human behaviour differ from probability in the "hard" sciences? Egan calls it a challenging time to enter the helping professions and welcomes readers to the profession and its debates.
sections.simple: Besides basic problem management, there are hundreds of ready-made programmes. Evidence-supported treatments (ESTs) are research-validated, manualised treatments, such as those for phobias; Barlow's unified 'transdiagnostic' protocol has seven modules. ESTs face criticism for targeting isolated symptoms rather than problems in living, so Egan recommends a both-and approach: use ESTs where they help, alongside the basics.
keyPoints: Hundreds of ready-made therapy and well-being programmes complement basic helping skills.
ESTs: validated by rigorous research, with step-by-step manuals; e.g. treatments for almost every phobia.
David Barlow is a pioneer; his unified 'transdiagnostic' protocol has seven modules.
Backlash stems from professional politics over ESTs' 'place'; ESTs tend to target isolated symptoms.
Egan favours a both-and (not either-or) approach to common factors and ESTs, based on client needs.
Open debates: medical model, client vs treatment emphasis, economics and third-party payers, probability in human behaviour.

sections.heading: General Well-Being Programs: Nutrition, Exercise, and Stress Reduction
sections.detailed:
Adjuncts to helping. Some programmes that promote general well-being can be used alongside every approach to helping. Ready-made programmes help people improve their quality of life by eating well, exercising and reducing stress; Egan cites a range of sources for each (for stress reduction, for example, Benson's work).

Self-regulation. All well-being programmes demand self-regulation, which many clients sorely need.

Social reasons. Researchers indicate that if people ate properly, exercised regularly and reduced and managed stress, the national health-care bill would fall by over 30%. Clients who manage stress well also have a better chance of dealing with problem situations.

The literature. Changing Unhealthy Habits, a 2007 supplement to the Mayo Clinic Health Letter, typifies the practical, science-based literature behind such programmes. Harvard Medical School publishes special reports on mental health, including stress management. Such literature reviews research and packages results practically for practitioners and clients. There is a rich literature on ready-made and well-being programmes; for example, a mindfulness website lists hundreds of articles by year. Egan tells readers the literature is theirs to devour.

Closing: talk is not change. The three stages of problem management are planning for life-enhancing change, but talk is not change; change requires action. That is why the book has stressed how each stage and task should stimulate client action. Endless sessions that only discuss problems and "consider" changes are, in Egan's words, "a lot of blah, blah, blah." Introducing a feedback system into therapy is one of the best ways to ensure talk leads to action. The final chapter deals formally with implementation, though Egan hopes the book has been about implementation throughout.
sections.simple: Well-being programmes for nutrition, exercise and stress reduction can support any kind of helping. They require self-regulation, and research suggests healthy habits could cut national health costs by over 30%. Egan ends by stressing that talk is not change; action is needed, and feedback systems help turn talk into action.
keyPoints: Nutrition, exercise and stress-reduction programmes are adjuncts to all approaches to helping.
All well-being programmes demand self-regulation.
Healthy eating, exercise and stress management could cut the national health-care bill by over 30%.
Practical literature: Mayo Clinic's 'Changing Unhealthy Habits' (2007), Harvard Medical School reports.
Talk is not change; a feedback system helps ensure talk leads to action; next chapter covers implementation.

terms.definition: The final stage of Egan's problem-management model, concerned with the activities needed to reach goals: developing strategies, choosing best-fit strategies and forming plans; it adds the 'game plan' to the client's change programme.
Broadly, all the work of Stages II and III (big-S and small-s solutions); narrowly, identifying, choosing and organising the strategies needed to accomplish goals.
Egan's phrase for what Stage III is about: the client's intended activities for producing goal outcomes, leading on to implementation itself.

Action is what the client does; the outcome is what is accomplished; impact is the constructive effect on the client's life. Action is valuable only if it leads to outcomes, and outcomes only if they have impact.
Helping clients develop a range of possible strategies for accomplishing their goals: 'What kind of actions will help me get what I need and want?'
Helping clients choose strategies that are effective, efficient and tailored to their preferences and resources: 'What actions are best for me?'
Helping clients turn strategies into a realistic plan: what to do first, second, and when to start.
Actions that help clients accomplish their goals.
The art of identifying and choosing realistic courses of action for achieving goals under adverse conditions, such as war; clients' problem situations are such conditions.
Imaginative thinking that generates many different routes to a goal; most clients do not do this instinctively, so helpers stimulate it.
Generating many possible strategies before choosing; it must be focused, since people decide better when they can choose among options.
A technique in which the helper offers a few possibilities or mentions what others have tried, then 'fades' so the client weighs, chooses and commits; it keeps suggestions from becoming advice.
Simple structures for probes that direct clients to resources: individuals, models and exemplars, communities, places, things, organisations, programmes and personal resources.
People who are already doing what the client wants to do, whose example suggests strategies.
Carkhuff's (1971) term for using skills training as part of therapy; it may be essential for clients whose problems stem from lack of life or coping skills.
The understanding and life skills a client needs to reach a goal; asking clients to act without them compounds the problem.
The strategy or 'package' of strategies that best suits the client's situation, resources, personality and preferences.
Goals that serve as means to a broader goal; for Bud, finding support and helping others served the broad goal of emotional stability.
Like goals, strategies should be specific, robust, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective and in keeping with the client's values.
Strategies concrete enough to drive behaviour.
As used in Stacy's case, a euphemism for having a patient follow the hospital's general routine; non-specific and inadequate for her needs.
Strategies that, when implemented, actually achieve the goal; they may be big or small.
Strategies that can be carried out with the client's resources, are under the client's control and are unencumbered by obstacles.
Trying out some possible strategies before choosing; useful, though some clients may use it to put off action.
A decision aid that weighs the benefits and costs of a choice, how acceptable or unacceptable each is, for the client and significant others; often best used as a mental filter that yields probes.
A record kept to discover patterns of cynicism and irritation in one's life; one of the strategies Clint chose.
Catching oneself in the act of indulging in hostile thoughts, or thoughts that lead to hostile feelings, and stopping them.
Choosing a course of action that might achieve a goal regardless of risk, cost or probability of success.
Choosing only low-risk courses of action with a high probability of at least limited success.
Choosing means likely to avoid the worst possible result, minimising the maximum danger, often without naming it.
Choosing strategies that balance risks against the probability of success; the ideal but most difficult approach.
A clear step-by-step process for accomplishing a goal; the sequence of actions that turns a goal into an outcome.
Informal plans, made throughout the helping process, for reaching 'little objectives' within a larger change programme.
A plan that divides strategies into workable steps, orders them, and assigns a timetable for each step.
Small manageable steps that keep clients from being overwhelmed and make goals doable.
Intermediate goals that move a client step by step toward a complex or difficult ultimate goal.
What makes a plan drive action: concrete activities, a logical but flexible sequence, and a time frame for each key step.
A mind-set, present from the first session, that sees clients as self-healing agents and keeps possible goals, strategies and plans in view without imposing preset programmes.
Alternative goals or strategies held in reserve, answering 'What will I do if my plan is not working?'
Ready-made, research-validated treatment programmes for mental health problems, with step-by-step manuals for training and clinical use.
Barlow and associates' unified set of principles drawn from what successful treatments of emotional disorders share, adaptable to any client; it has seven modules.
Egan's stance that common-factors helping and ESTs should be combined according to client needs, not treated as either-or.
Ready-made programmes for nutrition, exercise and stress reduction that can be adjuncts to any approach to helping; they demand self-regulation.

studies.title: Decision making with options
studies.finding: People tend to make better decisions when they can choose among a number of options, which is why brainstorming strategies helps.

studies.title: Goslin's decision-making pitfalls
studies.finding: People avoid unpleasant eventualities, struggle to value alternatives, close prematurely, undervalue long-range consequences, are swayed by the first formulation, overweight certain risks, are manipulable when values are unclear, and do not know when to seek more information; later research confirmed these pitfalls are prevalent.

studies.title: Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey on risk and probability
studies.finding: Clients deal with risk and probability by wishful thinking, playing it safe or avoiding the worst outcome; the ideal combination approach balances risk against probability of success.

studies.title: Millennium survey of about two million US employees
studies.finding: Its summary concluded that "People join companies but leave supervisors," which made Vince wary of supervisors who alienate their teams.

studies.title: Kirschenbaum on flexible planning
studies.finding: Being less specific and rigid about actions, sequence and deadlines can, in some cases, encourage people to keep choosing activities flexibly and become more self-reliant.

studies.title: Rigid planning and short-term goals
studies.finding: Rigid planning strategies can lead to frequent failure to achieve short-term goals; most people sit at the 'I hate all this detail' end of the continuum.

studies.title: Evidence-supported treatments
studies.finding: ESTs are validated by rigorous research; ESTs exist for almost every type of phobia.

studies.title: Barlow's unified protocol
studies.finding: Combines three or four concepts common to successful treatments of emotional disorders into a seven-module transdiagnostic protocol that Barlow says gives more flexibility than most manuals.

studies.title: Health-care costs and healthy habits
studies.finding: Researchers indicate that proper eating, regular exercise and stress management would reduce the national health-care bill by over 30%.

examples.title: Action, outcome and impact for a PG student
examples.text: A student preparing for a university exam makes a daily timetable and solves past papers (action), scores well in the semester exam (outcome), and feels confident enough to apply for a research assistantship (impact). If she studied hard without deciding what score or result she wanted, she would be like Lacy in her relationship: lots of activity, no clear outcome.

examples.title: Prompt and fade in a college counselling centre
examples.text: A first-year student wants to make friends in a new city. The counsellor says, 'Some students in your position have tried joining a college club, a sports team or a volunteer group. Do any of these sound right, or do they give you ideas of your own?' The counsellor then steps back and lets the student pick and commit.

examples.title: Using the strategy framework for a career change
examples.text: Someone wanting to move from accounting to counselling could ask: Which individuals (a counsellor relative)? Which models (someone who made the switch)? Which communities (a peer-support group)? Which places (a university counselling centre)? Which things (books, online courses)? Which organisations (an NGO helpline)? Which programmes (a diploma course)?

examples.title: Balance sheet for moving to a hostel
examples.text: A student deciding whether to move into a hostel lists benefits (more study time, independence) and costs (expense, missing family) for herself and for her parents, and asks which of each are acceptable or unacceptable. Often a counsellor just asks, 'How would your parents feel about this?', a probe that comes straight from the balance sheet.

examples.title: Shaping a plan with sequence and time frame
examples.text: A student who wants to clear an entrance exam lists what to do (revise syllabus, take mock tests, join a study group), decides the order (finish basic revision before mock tests) and sets a time frame (revision by month two, weekly mocks after that). Like Harriet, doing mocks before revising would waste effort.

examples.title: A contingency plan for admissions
examples.text: 'If I don't get into the MPhil programme, I will take a counselling job and reapply next year.' Like Egan's medical-school versus nurse-practitioner example, the backup keeps the student moving if the first plan fails.

checks.q: In Egan's narrower sense, planning refers to:
options: Identifying, choosing and organising the strategies needed to accomplish goals
All of Stages I, II and III
Setting goals that are powerfully imagined
Implementing the plan in the client's world
checks.explain: Broadly planning covers Stages II and III; narrowly it means identifying, choosing and organising strategies (p. 343).

checks.q: In Lacy's case, her seven months of sobriety is an example of:
checks.explain: Her AA attendance and phone calls were actions; staying sober for over seven months was the outcome; feeling better and making friends was the impact (p. 343).

checks.q: Mara's first goal concerns:
options: Establishing or entering a community with something like the spirit she found in Iran
checks.explain: Her first goal deals with her social life and community; the second with work, the third with her parents (p. 346).

checks.q: What effect did the crisis with her father have on Mara, according to Carlos?
options: It deepened her low-grade depression permanently
It made her decide to move to Iran
It made her abandon her goals
It seemed to energise her, leaving her freer and more determined
checks.explain: Carlos noticed the crisis somehow energised her; it was as if it swept the cobwebs out (p. 345).

checks.q: Egan describes Task III-A, developing a range of possible strategies, as:
checks.explain: Clients hemmed in by problems are liberated by defining the way forward, which builds self-efficacy (p. 346).

checks.q: According to Egan, strategy is the art of choosing realistic courses of action:
options: Only after goals have been abandoned
Under adverse conditions, such as war
Under the direction of the helper
checks.explain: Strategy involves identifying and choosing realistic courses of action under adverse conditions such as war (p. 346).

checks.q: The 'fade' part of the prompt-and-fade technique serves to:
options: Keep the helper's suggestions from becoming advice-giving
checks.explain: The fade keeps it clear that the client must think the strategies over, choose and commit (pp. 347-348).

checks.q: Which strategy did Elton's peers Jerry and Philomena model?
options: Video-recording every session for the supervisor
Competing for the best grade in practicum
Avoiding personal issues in practice sessions
A 5-10 minute review before each session of where the client is in the helping process
checks.explain: Jerry and Philomena spend 5 or 10 minutes before each session reviewing where the client is and how to add value (p. 348).

checks.q: Which resource category in Egan's framework does Jackson's co-worker, who died of cancer at home, represent?
checks.explain: Models and exemplars are people presently doing what the client wants to do (pp. 349-350).

checks.q: For Jackson, the hospice with three programmes is an example of which framework category?
checks.explain: Programs asks whether there are ready-made programmes for people in the client's position; the hospice's goals were practically the same as Jackson's (p. 350).

checks.q: Carkhuff's phrase 'training as treatment' refers to:
options: Treating clients by training them to be counsellors
Using skills training as part of therapy
checks.explain: Egan cites Carkhuff (1971) for skills training as part of therapy, which may be essential for some clients (p. 351).

checks.q: In the marriage counsellor's group programme, in what order are partners paired for practice?
options: Mixed pairs first, then same-sex pairs
Same-sex pairs, then mixed pairs of non-spouses, then spouses
checks.explain: He pairs woman with woman and man with man, then a man and woman who are not spouses, and finally spouses (p. 352).

checks.q: In Task III-B, clients need to choose strategies that best fit their:
checks.explain: Clients choose a strategy or package that best fits their situation, resources, personality and preferences (p. 352).

checks.q: Why does Egan add Task III-B to the helping process?
options: Some clients need help choosing which strategies best fit their situation
Clients cannot implement plans without it
checks.explain: Some clients move ahead alone, but others need help choosing; brainstorming is useless if clients don't know what to do with the results (p. 352).

checks.q: Bud's two broad strategies for achieving emotional stability were:
checks.explain: Finding support and helping others cope, instrumental goals, were his best strategies (p. 353).

checks.q: Who helped Bud see his need for social support?
checks.explain: Sandra believed many patients were hospitalised for lack of support and helped Bud see his need for it (p. 353).

checks.q: Why did milieu therapy fail Stacy?
options: It was not specific to her needs and no therapeutic goals were set
It forced her into the community too early
checks.explain: Milieu therapy was a general programme, not specific to her needs, with no goals set (p. 354).

checks.q: Strategies are 'effective' when they:
options: Actually achieve the goal when implemented
checks.explain: Effectiveness means the strategy actually achieves the goal; strategies can be big or small (p. 354).

checks.q: According to Egan, strategies are realistic when they:
options: Involve no stretch for the client
Are approved by the client's family
Can be carried out with the client's resources, are under the client's control and are free of obstacles
checks.explain: This is Egan's three-part definition of realistic strategies (p. 355).

checks.q: What helped Desmond eventually get a suitable job?
options: Applying to many jobs at random
A self-help group for laid-off managers
A university outreach programme linking him with supportive companies
checks.explain: A counsellor from a university outreach programme connected him with companies with programmes for people with psychiatric problems (p. 355).

checks.q: In the case of the priest unjustly accused, what did the counsellor do about the lawyer's tactics?
options: Helped the priest clarify and challenge his values without imposing anyone's values
Advised him to follow the lawyer
Told him to drop the lawyer
checks.explain: The counsellor helped him clarify and challenge his values but did not impose his own or the lawyer's (p. 356).

checks.q: Which of these is a question in Box 13.2 on best-fit strategies?
options: What are the different routes for getting there?
Which strategies will have the fewest unwanted consequences?
Which step of the program needs substeps?
What do I need to do later?
checks.explain: Box 13.2 includes fewest unwanted consequences; the others come from Boxes 13.1 and 13.3 (p. 356).

checks.q: Which options did the two feuding business partners sample?
options: A therapist, a priest and a mediator
A lawyer, a consultant-counsellor and an arbitration firm
A coach, an accountant and a banker
checks.explain: They discussed court with a lawyer, met a consultant-counsellor and visited an arbitration firm, then chose the consultant-counsellor (p. 356).

checks.q: What risk of strategy sampling does Egan mention?
options: It makes clients dependent on the helper
Some clients could use it to put off action
checks.explain: Egan notes some clients could use sampling to postpone action, though not Bud (p. 357).

checks.q: The balance-sheet method weighs:
options: Benefits and costs, and their acceptability and unacceptability, for self and significant others
Only the financial costs of therapy
Strengths and weaknesses of the helper
checks.explain: Balance sheets deal with the acceptability and unacceptability of both benefits and costs, to self and significant others (p. 357).

checks.q: According to Egan, one of the best ways to use the balance sheet is:
options: To have every client fill it in for every decision
Not to use it directly, but to keep it in mind as a filter and turn parts into probes
Only for the decision to begin therapy
checks.explain: He advises keeping it in the back of your mind, listening through it and turning parts into probes; 'No formula' (p. 358).

checks.q: Which set of strategies did Clint choose for his 'experiment'?
options: Talking to a counsellor, keeping a hostility log, thought stopping and talking sense to himself
checks.explain: Clint chose a counsellor, a hostility log, thought stopping and self-talk (p. 359).

checks.q: Why did Clint's counsellor not challenge him early?
options: He agreed Clint's attitudes needed no change
He was waiting for Clint's doctor
He bet that through strategy sampling Clint would discover the problem went deeper
checks.explain: The counsellor relied on strategy sampling to teach Clint more about his problem (p. 359).

checks.q: Jenny, who nags her ex-husband for more support without considering risk, cost or probability, illustrates:
checks.explain: Wishful thinking chooses a course of action regardless of risk, cost or probability (p. 359).

checks.q: Crissy's 'assertiveness', which is really compliance with frills, is driven by:
options: Wishful thinking about her husband changing
Avoiding the worst outcome of losing her partner
checks.explain: Her unnamed maximum danger is losing her partner, so she minimises that danger (p. 360).

checks.q: The ideal 'combination' approach to choosing strategies:
options: Balances risks against the probability of success
checks.explain: In the ideal case clients balance risk against probability of success; it is the most difficult approach (p. 360).

checks.q: Which of these is NOT listed as required by the combination approach?
checks.explain: It requires analysis, goals with the right edge, clear values, ranking strategies, estimating effectiveness and challenging blind spots; not avoiding risk (pp. 360-361).

checks.q: What did Frank lack that kept him stuck?
options: An overall programme with specific milestones
checks.explain: Frank had inventive strategies but could never be pinned down to an overall programme with milestones (p. 362).

checks.q: Why does Egan call Roseanne a 'coconspirator'?
options: She told Vince about Frank's weaknesses
She relished their business discussions and never challenged Frank
She designed a plan that was too rigid
She encouraged Frank to leave the company
checks.explain: She too enjoyed the business talk and failed to challenge him (p. 362).

checks.q: Tess contacting her friend Lou for support is an example of:
checks.explain: Egan calls this a 'little plan' that is part of her overall change programme (p. 362).

checks.q: Walter's case illustrates that plans:
options: Make clients aware of social support needs
Provide an opportunity to evaluate the realism and adequacy of goals
checks.explain: While planning, Walter saw that getting his job back and winning a countersuit were unrealistic (p. 363).

checks.q: A well-shaped plan answers which three questions?
options: What must be done, in what sequence, and in what time frame
What is the problem, what is the goal, what is the cost
How specific, how rigid, how soon
checks.explain: A plan should say what concrete things must be done, in what order and when (p. 364).

checks.q: Egan's view on plan complexity is that:
options: Complicated plans broken into subgoals can be as achievable as simple ones if the time frame is realistic
checks.explain: Simpler is generally better, but what matters is whether the plan is well shaped (p. 364).

checks.q: Harriet's main planning mistake was:
options: Taking relevant courses out of optimal sequence
Taking too many courses at once
checks.explain: She took Social Problem-Solving Skills before the communication course it assumed (p. 365).

checks.q: Which course would have helped Harriet most in the peer-helper programme?
checks.explain: She realised developmental psychology would have helped her understand herself and her peers (p. 365).

checks.q: In the revisited plan, what is Frank's first step?
options: Asking each subordinate what they need from him and what style would help them
Sending a memo on stretch goals
checks.explain: He first calls in each subordinate to ask what they need; the memo on objectives is the second step (p. 365).

checks.q: Frank's revisited plan would only have worked on condition that:
options: He was convinced the new approach made personal and business sense
checks.explain: Egan adds the condition that Frank was convinced a different approach made sense (p. 366).

checks.q: Why do Stages II and III need a 'human face'?
options: Helpers who are pedantic or mechanistic risk alienating clients, while skipping these steps shortchanges them
checks.explain: Egan warns against both skipping planning and being mechanistic (pp. 366-367).

checks.q: Cora's progress in counselling is described as a change of identity from:
options: Battered woman to survivor to doer
checks.explain: Further sessions helped her move from battered woman to survivor and eventually to doer (p. 367).

checks.q: Kirschenbaum's three questions concern:
options: How specific activities must be, how rigid the order must be, and how soon each must be done
Wishful thinking, playing it safe and avoiding the worst
checks.explain: Kirschenbaum (1985) proposed these questions to challenge blueprint planning (p. 367).

checks.q: Yousef's case shows that:
options: Small informal changes, without formal planning, can still produce constructive change
Clients should be referred to ready-made programmes
checks.explain: Yousef never discussed an extensive programme but made small changes; his counsellor had a constructive-change mentality without formal planning (p. 368).

checks.q: Why does a helper offer a plan as a sketch rather than a detailed programme?
options: Because detailed plans are always wrong
So the client can fill it out and adapt it, growing in self-determination
checks.explain: The aim is not dependence but self-determination; clients fill out and tailor the outline (p. 369).

checks.q: According to Egan, the final arbiter of a plan's effectiveness is:
options: The amount of detail in the plan
checks.explain: There is no good plan in itself; outcomes, not planning or hard work, are the final arbiter (p. 369).

checks.q: Backup plans help clients avoid which trap?
checks.explain: Backup plans give flexibility and keep clients from the status quo trap (p. 370).

checks.q: In Linda's case, obtaining political refugee status or a green card are examples of:
options: Instrumental goals that serve as fall-back options
checks.explain: Her lawyer friend helped her review instrumental goals toward her ultimate goal of living in the US (p. 370).

checks.q: How many modules does Barlow's unified protocol have?
checks.explain: The seven modules run from psychoeducation to relapse prevention (p. 371).

checks.q: One criticism of ESTs mentioned by Egan is that they:
options: Tend to deal with isolated symptoms rather than problems in living
checks.explain: ESTs tend to target isolated symptoms, and no ready-made programme fits a complex couple's problems (p. 371).

checks.q: All general well-being programmes demand:
checks.explain: Egan says all well-being programmes demand self-regulation, sorely needed by many clients (p. 372).

checks.q: What does Egan say is one of the best ways to ensure talk leads to action?
options: Introducing a feedback system into therapy
Using the balance sheet with every client
checks.explain: Introducing a feedback system is one of the best ways to assure talk leads to action (p. 372).

practice.q: Define strategy as used in Egan's Stage III.
practice.answer: Egan defines strategies as actions that help clients accomplish their goals. More broadly, strategy is the art of identifying and choosing realistic courses of action for reaching goals under adverse conditions, such as war. Clients' problem situations are themselves adverse conditions, so developing strategies is a humane and liberating part of helping.

practice.q: What is the 'prompt and fade' technique?
practice.answer: Prompt and fade is a way for helpers to offer suggestions while keeping the client in charge. The helper prompts by offering a few possibilities or describing what others with similar problems have tried, then fades, so the client weighs the options, chooses and commits. The fade keeps it from becoming advice-giving.

practice.q: Distinguish action, outcome and impact.
practice.answer: Action is what the client does, the outcome is what that action achieves, and impact is the constructive effect on the client's life. In Lacy's case, attending AA was action, seven months' sobriety was the outcome, and feeling better and rebuilding her social life was the impact. Action is valuable only if it leads to outcomes with impact.

practice.q: What did Carkhuff mean by 'training as treatment'?
practice.answer: Carkhuff (1971) used 'training as treatment' for skills training used as part of therapy. Many clients get into or stay in trouble because they lack life or coping skills, so teaching those skills is an important broad strategy. Asking clients to act without the necessary skills compounds the problem.

practice.q: What is strategy sampling?
practice.answer: Strategy sampling means trying out some possible strategies before choosing among them. Two feuding business partners sampled a lawyer, a consultant-counsellor and an arbitration firm before choosing the consultant-counsellor; sampling also let their emotions cool. Egan warns that some clients may use sampling to put off action.

practice.q: What are contingency plans?
practice.answer: Contingency or backup plans are alternative goals or strategies kept ready in case the chosen plan fails or circumstances change. They answer 'What will I do if my plan is not working?', give freedom and flexibility, help avoid the status quo trap and build responsibility. They can be as simple as asking 'If that doesn't work, then what?'

practice.q: What are evidence-supported treatments (ESTs)?
practice.answer: ESTs are ready-made treatment programmes for mental health problems, designed by researchers and practitioners and validated by rigorous research. They come with step-by-step manuals for training and clinical use; ESTs exist for almost every type of phobia. Egan names David Barlow as a pioneer of evidence-based practice.

practice.q: Explain the balance-sheet method for choosing strategies.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan borrows the idea of a balance sheet, which in business deals with the economics of an enterprise, and applies it to the economics of problem management. It can be used for any key decision in helping, such as whether to seek help, which problem to tackle, which goal to set or which strategy to choose.

The questions. The method weighs both benefits and costs, and asks how acceptable and how unacceptable each is, both for the client and for significant others. Applied to a strategy, the client asks: What are the benefits of this strategy for me and for others? To what degree are they acceptable, and in what ways are they unacceptable? What are the costs for me and for others? To what degree are they acceptable, and in what ways unacceptable?

Illustration. Karen, an alcoholic with a husband and three teenagers, considered a one-month residential treatment programme but wondered if it was self-indulgent. Her counsellor Joan helped her complete a balance sheet covering the effects on her family, her workplace and herself ('What will people think? What if I fail?'). Karen concluded the residential programme was more substantial than outpatient care and would help her most, and Joan then helped her plan how to address the pain she was causing others.

Using it flexibly. Egan warns against using it with every client or every decision; it should be used when helper and client think it will help, and tailored to the client. Often the best use is indirect: the helper keeps the balance sheet in mind as a listening filter and turns parts of it into probes, such as 'How will this affect your husband?' or 'Is there any downside to that strategy?' There is no formula.

Conclusion. The balance sheet helps clients make more considered choices by bringing costs, benefits and effects on others into view.

practice.q: Describe the use of frameworks to help clients develop strategies, with reference to the case of Jackson.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan says helpers can use simple frameworks to frame probes that help clients generate a range of strategies. The framework directs clients to the resources in their lives.

Jackson's goals. Jackson has terminal cancer and probably less than a year to live. He wants to die outside hospital, as peacefully as possible and with his faculties intact.

The framework categories.
- Individuals: a doctor who teaches pain-management techniques, his wife and daughter learning to give injections, and a trusted friend whose wife died of cancer.
- Models and exemplars: a co-worker who died at home and refused 'poor-me' talk, giving Jackson both the idea and an attitude to imitate.
- Communities: his parish's services for the sick and online self-help groups.
- Places: a possible pilgrimage to Lourdes, and an Internet chat room where he can sometimes be a helper.
- Things: drug combinations and electrical stimulation for pain, explored with his doctor and second opinions.
- Organisations: an Internet-based support organisation where he volunteers and receives as much as he gives (Mara similarly explores PARSA and Iranian Alliances Across Borders).
- Programs: a hospice with three programmes whose goals match his.

Box 13.1. Clients can also ask themselves questions such as: What are the different routes to my destination? How many ways are there to reach my goals? What can I do right away, and what later?

Conclusion. Frameworks turn vague wishes into concrete options by systematically surveying the client's resources.

practice.q: Discuss Bud's amazing odyssey as an illustration of best-fit strategies.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan opens Task III-B with Bud, whose two best-fit strategies produced results beyond anyone's expectations.

Background. At 18 Bud woke unable to speak or move and was diagnosed with catatonic schizophrenia; after repeated hospital stays with drugs and ECT, the diagnosis became paranoid schizophrenia and he was considered incurable. His history showed unmanaged life problems and lack of support: separation from his mother for four years, harassment at school for his 'ethnic' looks and accent, and too much change. The clock change from daylight saving time seemed the last straw.

Turning point. In hospital Bud came to believe patients could do something about their illnesses and found the drug and ECT 'help' debilitating. He left, got a job and married. When readmitted after stress, he met Sandra, a psychiatric social worker who believed lack of support kept many patients ill. She showed him his need for support and noticed his knack for helping others.

Strategies. Bud's broad goal was emotional stability. His two strategies, which were also instrumental goals, were finding support and helping others. He had Sandra coach his wife to support him under stress, started a self-help group for ex-patients and developed it into a network of groups.

Lesson. Bud translated one broad goal into practical goals, found two broad strategies, made them concrete and achieved stability. His case is not the norm, but it shows the power of problem management joined to self-responsibility. Later in the chapter it also illustrates specific strategies, strategy sampling, bite-size steps and subgoals.

practice.q: Explain the three pitfalls in selecting strategies identified by Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan says the shadow side of decision making affects how clients choose strategies; they often fail to weigh risk against the probability of success. Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey (1972) described three ways clients handle risk and probability. Clients use these without reflection, which is why they lie in the shadows.

1. Wishful thinking. The client chooses an action that might, they hope, work, regardless of risk, cost or probability. Jenny nags her ex-husband to pay more support, ignoring the risk that he stops paying, the emotional cost and the low chance of success. Clients who work hard but get nowhere may be doing this; helpers should challenge it, for instance by asking Jenny to review how well her approach has worked.

2. Playing it safe. The client picks only low-risk actions likely to give at least limited success. Liam, unhappy with his boss, drops hints, jokes and lets himself be intimidated in appraisals instead of raising his concerns, believing he is being 'reasonable'.

3. Avoiding the worst outcome. The client chooses means that minimise the maximum danger, often without naming it. Crissy's 'assertiveness' is compliance with frills because her unspoken fear is losing her husband; a counsellor's probe that 'Bill has you just where he wants you' startles her into realism.

Striking a balance. The ideal is a combination approach that balances risk against probability of success. It is the hardest, requiring good analysis, clear values, ranked strategies and challenge to blind spots, which helpers should help capable clients do.

practice.q: Discuss how helpers can help clients develop contingency plans.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Because the future is uncertain, Egan advises keeping a broad range of options open. Investing heavily in a goal or programme that must later change is wasteful, so helpers help clients choose backup goals and plans.

Value of contingency. Clients then have both direction and contingency: if the world changes, they choose the goal that best fits. Choosing a goal is not a once-and-forever decision; the client sticks with it until it stops being viable or a better one emerges. Viable options make it easier to drop a failing option, give freedom and flexibility, and protect against the status quo decision-making trap.

Linda's case. Linda, raised in Iraq, now in Mexico after a dangerous journey as an illegal immigrant, wants to live permanently in the United States and plans to do so illegally. Her lawyer friend helps her review instrumental goals: political refugee status, a green card, marrying a US citizen or a foreigner likely to get a green card, or entering the skilled-immigrant quota. Each would need its own plan, and she now has fall-back options.

Contingency in strategies. Strategies as well as goals may need changing. Contingency plans answer 'What will I do if my plan is not working?', make clients better tacticians, are especially needed for high-risk programmes aimed at critical goals, and build responsibility because clients must decide when to switch.

Conclusion. Backup plans need not be complicated; the helper may simply ask, 'If that doesn't work, then what will you do?'

practice.q: Explain the role of working knowledge and skills in Stage III.
practice.answer:
Introduction. People often get into trouble, or fail to escape it, because they lack the life or coping skills their problems demand. Helping clients learn these skills is therefore an important broad strategy.

Training as treatment. Egan cites Carkhuff's (1971) term 'training as treatment': skills training as part of therapy may be essential for some clients. Challenging clients to act when they lack the skills compounds rather than solves their problems. The helper therefore asks what working knowledge and skills the client needs to reach the goal.

Jerzy and Zelda. After a two-year honeymoon period, this couple began fighting about finances, sex and values once romantic fervour cooled. They lacked interpersonal communication skills, did not understand each other's developmental needs across their nine-year age gap (a 20-year-old wife and a 29-year-old husband), and had few problem-solving skills. Egan notes that lack of communication and other life skills is often at the heart of relationship breakdowns.

A group programme. A marriage counsellor works with four couples at a time. He separates men and women and trains them in tuning in, active listening and empathic responding, pairing same-sex partners, then non-spouse mixed pairs, then spouses. Spouses then learn a simple version of the problem-management process and use their skills to solve problems together.

Conclusion. Equipping clients with interpersonal communication and problem-solving skills serves the second goal of helping described in Chapter 1.

practice.q: Describe how formal plans add value to clients' change programmes.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Some clients plan on their own; others need help, and some clients and helpers underrate plans, so Egan reviews their advantages. He distinguishes 'little plans', informal steps toward little objectives (Tess enlisting her friend Lou for support), from formal plans, which divide strategies into workable steps, order them and set a timetable for each.

Advantages of formal planning.
1. Discipline: planning makes reasonable demands on clients who lack discipline; Desmond benefited from a formal job-seeking programme, and AA's 12 steps encourage self-discipline.
2. Avoiding overwhelm: bite-size steps make goals doable; Bud began by joining one self-help group.
3. Better strategies: planning showed Sy Johnson's family their coping had been hit-or-miss, and with Al-Anon they started afresh.
4. Testing goals: planning showed Walter that getting his job back and winning a countersuit were unrealistic, so he revised them.
5. Resources: planning showed Dora she lacked social support, so a goal of getting back into community was added.
6. Hidden obstacles: planning his social life revealed Ernesto's shame over accidentally killing a bystander.

Conclusion. Plans do not solve everything, but they make time an ally rather than an enemy and replace aimless activity. Egan notes planning also has a shadow side (Dorner, 1996).

practice.q: Write a note on ready-made action programmes.
practice.answer:
Introduction. The book focuses on basic problem management for messy problems in living, but there are hundreds of ready-made therapy and well-being programmes that complement basic skills. Egan names and briefly describes two kinds.

Evidence-supported treatments. ESTs are research-validated programmes for mental health problems with step-by-step manuals; there are ESTs for almost every phobia. David Barlow is a pioneer. Many are simple, but some are complex, such as Barlow and associates' unified 'transdiagnostic' protocol for depression, anxiety and phobias. Its seven modules are psychoeducation, motivational enhancement, emotional awareness training, cognitive appraisal and reappraisal, modifying emotion-driven behaviours and avoidance, exposure to emotional experience, and relapse prevention.

Debate. There has been a backlash, driven by professional politics over where ESTs belong, and because they tend to address isolated symptoms rather than problems in living. Egan advocates a both-and approach: use relevant ESTs alongside common-factors helping as the client needs.

General well-being programmes. Programmes for nutrition, exercise and stress reduction can be adjuncts to any helping. They demand self-regulation. Researchers suggest healthy habits could cut the national health-care bill by over 30%, and clients who manage stress cope better. Sources include the Mayo Clinic's 'Changing Unhealthy Habits' and Harvard Medical School reports.

Conclusion. Egan closes by reminding readers that talk is not change; action, supported by feedback, is what matters.

practice.q: Discuss Stage III of Egan's problem-management model.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Stage III, 'Planning the Way Forward', completes the planning part of Egan's problem-management model. Broadly, planning includes all of Stages II and III; narrowly, it means identifying, choosing and organising the strategies needed to accomplish goals. Stage II concerns outcomes, goals that have been powerfully imagined; Stage III concerns the activities that produce them, or 'implementation intentions'.

Action, outcome and impact. Egan stresses that action is valuable only if it leads to outcomes, and outcomes only if they have a constructive impact. Lacy's AA activities (action) produced seven months' sobriety (outcome) and a renewed life (impact), whereas her many actions in an abusive relationship produced nothing until she defined the outcome she wanted.

Task III-A: possible strategies. Strategies are actions that help clients reach goals, and developing a range of them is an exercise in liberation that boosts self-efficacy. Helpers stimulate divergent thinking through focused brainstorming (Mara's list of ways to build a social life), using 'prompt and fade' so suggestions do not become advice. Simple frameworks direct clients to resources: individuals, models, communities, places, things, organisations and programmes, as in Jackson's search for ways to die outside hospital. Helpers also identify the working knowledge and skills clients need; Carkhuff called skills training 'training as treatment'.

Task III-B: best-fit strategies. Clients choose a strategy or package that fits their situation, resources, personality and preferences. Bud, once labelled incurable, achieved emotional stability through two strategies: finding support and helping others. Strategies should meet the same criteria as goals: specific, robust, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective and value-consistent. Stacy's vague milieu therapy failed, Desmond needed realistic help to find a supportive job, and a falsely accused priest refused tactics that violated his values. Clients may sample strategies before choosing, and the balance-sheet method helps weigh benefits and costs for self and others. Helpers must also link strategies to action, as with Clint's 'experiment'. The shadow side includes Goslin's decision pitfalls and the three pitfalls of wishful thinking, playing it safe and avoiding the worst outcome; the ideal is balancing risk against probability of success.

Task III-C: plans. Strategies are organised into a plan, a sequence of actions turning goals into outcomes. Frank's failure to commit to a plan with milestones cost him the presidency. Plans build discipline, keep steps bite-size, prompt better strategies, test goals, reveal needed resources and uncover hidden obstacles. A well-shaped plan says what to do, in what order and when; Harriet's poorly sequenced courses and Frank's imagined second chance illustrate this.

Humanising change. Egan offers four principles: build a planning mentality in from the start, adapt planning to the client's style (Kirschenbaum's flexible planning; Gitta versus Yousef), outline a plan and let the client tailor it (Katrina), and develop contingency plans (Linda). Ready-made programmes such as ESTs and well-being programmes complement the basics.

Conclusion. Stage III turns goals into a practical game plan, but planning is not action. Without action, a change programme is a wish list, and the final test of any plan is life-enhancing outcomes.

practice.q: Explain the criteria for choosing goal-accomplishing strategies with suitable illustrations from Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction. In Task III-B clients must choose the strategies that best fit them. Egan says the criteria for strategies resemble those for goals: strategies should be specific, robust, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective and in keeping with the client's values. Clients need not know all of these, but helpers must. Egan illustrates several.

Specific strategies. Strategies must be specific enough to drive behaviour. Bud's broad strategies of tapping human support and helping others became concrete actions: keeping in touch with Sandra, getting help from his wife, joining and then starting a self-help group, and founding a self-help organisation. Stacy, in contrast, diagnosed with schizophrenia after years of isolation following her husband's death, was put on 'milieu' therapy, simply following hospital routine, with no therapeutic goals. Being non-specific, it was totally inadequate and only marginally better than drug-focused care.

Effective strategies. Strategies are effective when they actually achieve the goal; they may be big or small. Stacy's original programme was too general and lacked bite. A new psychiatrist placed her in a comprehensive social-learning programme with cognitive restructuring, social-skills training and behavioural interventions using incentives, shaping, modelling and rewards. She was discharged within six months and stayed in the community. This programme met all the criteria; it was cost-effective because it made the best use of her resources and returned her and others to the community, and it fitted her real values of companionship and freedom.

Realistic strategies. Strategies are realistic when they can be carried out with the client's resources, are under the client's control and face no blocking obstacles. Desmond, living in a halfway house with recurrent depression, applied for jobs randomly and was always rejected. A university outreach programme connected him with companies that supported workers with psychiatric problems, and he found a suitable job. Egan adds that realism must not mean selling clients short; stretch strategies, like Bud's, can be very rewarding.

Strategies in keeping with values. A priest falsely accused of child molestation refused his lawyer's plan to dig up dirt on his accusers, saying it would lower him to their level. He built a fact-based case and was acquitted. His counsellor helped him clarify and challenge his values without imposing anyone's. Mara likewise sees that many of her strategies express a wish to reconnect with her Iranian roots. Box 13.2 offers questions such as which strategies best fit my resources, my preferred way of acting and my values, and which have the fewest unwanted consequences.

Sample, then choose. Some clients choose better after sampling. Two feuding business partners consulted a lawyer, a consultant-counsellor and an arbitration firm before choosing the counsellor, and sampling also calmed their emotions. Bud's attending a self-help group was sampling too. The risk is that sampling can be used to delay action.

The balance sheet. Clients can also weigh benefits and costs, their acceptability and unacceptability, for themselves and significant others, as Karen did in choosing residential treatment.

Conclusion. These criteria help clients choose strategies that are workable, effective and their own, so that chosen strategies are likely to be carried through into action.

practice.q: Discuss the shadow side of selecting strategies.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan reminds helpers that the shadow side of decision making operates whenever clients choose strategies. Clients often make choices without reflecting on what they are doing or on unintended consequences, and helpers must be alert to this.

Goslin's pitfalls. Egan cites Goslin (1985), whose early account of decision-making pitfalls has since been shown by research to be widespread. When defining problems, people dislike thinking about unpleasant possibilities, find it difficult to assign values to alternatives, tend toward premature closure, overlook or undervalue long-range consequences and are unduly influenced by the first way the problem is framed. When evaluating consequences they give extra weight to risks known with certainty, are more easily manipulated when their values are poorly thought through, and struggle to know when to seek more information. Above all, clients often fail to evaluate risk and to check whether it is balanced by the probability of success.

Three pitfalls. Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey (1972) described three ways clients deal with risk and probability.

Wishful thinking. The client chooses a course of action that might achieve the goal regardless of risk, cost or probability. Jenny tries to make her ex-husband pay more child support by nagging and guilt-tripping him. She ignores the risk that he may stop paying altogether, the cost in time and emotional energy, and the low chance of success given that he reacts badly to nagging. Such clients act blindly; at worst this is reckless. Clients who 'work hard' and 'get nowhere' may be persisting with preferred but doubtful means. Helpers should challenge this, inviting Jenny to review what she has done and how successful it has been.

Playing it safe. The client chooses only low-risk actions with a high probability of limited success. Liam, a manager in his 40s, wants to tell his boss of his dissatisfaction and learn about his career prospects. Yet he avoids the topic when the boss is in a bad mood and does not want to upset things when the mood is good. He drops hints, jokes, hopes word filters back and is intimidated in appraisals, all while seeing himself as reasonable. He does not realise how safe he is playing it.

Avoiding the worst outcome. The client chooses means that minimise the maximum danger, often without naming it. Crissy sets a goal to be more assertive, but her unspoken fear is losing her husband, so her assertiveness is compliance with frills, such as occasional evenings out that her husband actually enjoys. She avoids reviewing the relationship because it might be the beginning of the end. Her counsellor asks how she would react if a friend said 'Bill has you just where he wants you', which startles her into a more realistic view.

Striking a balance. The ideal, according to these authors, is a combination approach that balances risk against probability of success. It is the hardest because it requires sound analysis of problems and opportunities, goals with the right edge, clarity about values, ranking strategies by those values, estimating effectiveness and, above all, challenging blind spots.

Conclusion. These shadow-side tendencies operate silently, so helpers must recognise and challenge them, helping capable clients choose strategies that realistically balance risk and reward.

practice.q: Explain the principles for humanising the mechanics of constructive change.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan admits that real-world planning seldom resembles textbook planning. He recalls a friend who returned a detailed self-development book asking who would go through all that; Egan's retort was righteous rather than realistic. Most people are too impatient for detailed planning, and lack of planning discipline helps explain the dismal record of discretionary change. Stages II and III therefore need a human face. Helpers who skip goal setting and planning shortchange clients, but helpers who are pedantic or mechanistic risk alienating them. Egan offers four principles.

1. Build a planning mentality into helping from the start. A constructive-change mind-set should permeate helping from the first session. Helpers should see clients as self-healing agents, not just people stuck in problems. Even while listening to the story, they should think about remedies and probe the client's ideas for change, asking for instance what the client has already tried. Cora, a battered wife, learned about typical responses to battering, stopped blaming herself, confronted her husband, joined a self-help group and learned to use police and courts, moving from battered woman to survivor to doer. Such scenarios should be part of the helper's mentality, not imposed programmes.

2. Adapt the process to the client's style. Planning can be formal or informal. Kirschenbaum (1985) questioned blueprint planning and asked how specific activities must be, how rigid their order and how soon they must be done; he argued flexibility can make clients more self-reliant and proactive. Gitta, entering the empty nest, loved detailed planning because she had run her household that way. But most clients sit at the 'I hate all this detail' end, and rigid plans can lead to frequent failure of short-term goals. Yousef, a single father of a son with intellectual disability, made small informal changes, such as having a friend drop by and taking weekend outings, without any formal plan. A slipshod approach is also self-defeating. There are no formulas, only client needs, planning skills and common sense. In brief therapy, helpers should get clients acting quickly, then review and refine, asking what will add most value.

3. Outline a plan and help the client tailor it. Experienced helpers build a stockpile of programmes and can stitch pieces together for clients who lack the skills or temperament to plan. To promote self-determination rather than dependence, they offer a sketch for the client to fill out. Katrina, overweight, reclusive and depressed, received an outline including blame reduction, redefining beauty, reducing self-imposed restrictions, cognitive restructuring and obesity information, with detail added as she became involved. The final test of a plan is life-enhancing outcomes, not planning or hard work.

4. Help clients develop contingency plans. Because the future is uncertain, clients need backup goals and plans. These give freedom and flexibility, prevent the status quo trap and build responsibility. Linda, determined to live in the US, was helped to see legal routes such as refugee status, a green card, marriage or the skilled-immigrant quota. A simple 'If that doesn't work, then what?' can suffice.

Conclusion. These principles balance rigour and humanity, keeping planning useful without making it mechanical, and always aimed at action and outcomes.

practice.q: Discuss Task III-C: helping clients formulate viable plans.
practice.answer:
Introduction. After identifying and choosing strategies, clients must organise them into a plan. In Task III-C counsellors help clients come up with the sequence of actions, what first, what second, that turns a goal into an outcome. Egan admits that in practice this, like all problem-management tasks, is messy, so therapists must understand where clients are in the 'geography' of helping.

The cost of no plan: Frank. Frank, a vice president and heir apparent, was told by the president, Vince, that he needed to become a leader rather than a micromanaging operations man. Vince, influenced by a survey concluding that people join companies but leave supervisors, valued people-centred leadership. Frank hired a coach, Roseanne, and generated inventive strategies, but would never commit to a programme with milestones, calling it too stifling. He dabbled, and after two years someone else became president. Frank had two blind spots: he did not take Vince's idea of leadership seriously and thought marginal change would do. Roseanne, enjoying their business talk, never challenged him, making her a co-conspirator.

How plans add value. Plans may be informal 'little plans', like Tess enlisting her friend Lou's support, or formal plans that divide strategies into ordered, timetabled steps. Formal plans: (1) develop discipline, as with Desmond's job-seeking programme and AA's 12 steps; (2) prevent overwhelm through bite-size steps, as Bud began with one self-help group; (3) prompt better strategies, as with the Johnson family and Al-Anon; (4) test the realism of goals, as Walter revised his; (5) reveal needed resources, as Dora saw her need for social support; and (6) uncover hidden obstacles, as Ernesto discovered his shame. Plans make time an ally, though planning also has a shadow side (Dorner, 1996).

Shaping the plan. Plans need shape to drive action: they should state the concrete things to be done, their sequence and the time frame. Complex goals need subgoals; Bud's test group and 'charter in place' were subgoals toward his organisation. Simpler is generally better, but what matters is whether the plan is well shaped; complex plans broken into subgoals are achievable with a realistic time frame.

Harriet. Harriet, wanting to be a counsellor, took relevant courses in the wrong order, starting with problem-solving skills, which assumed the communication skills she had not yet learned, and volunteering as a peer helper without the developmental psychology that would have helped. With a psychologist she re-planned and sequenced her courses; better shaping would have made her programme more efficient.

Frank revisited. In a second chance, Frank's plan states what to do (involve subordinates, listen, set objectives through dialogue, delegate, coach, give feedback), the sequence (first ask each subordinate what they need, then set objectives including stretch goals through dialogue in the planning cycle) and the time frame (immediately, within three weeks, postponing delegation). This would work only if Frank believed in the change. Box 13.3 lists planning questions about sequence, critical actions, time frames, substeps, flexibility and resources.

Conclusion. Viable plans turn chosen strategies into ordered, timed actions. They are a means to action and outcomes, not ends in themselves.

summary: Narrowly, planning means identifying, choosing and organising strategies; Stage II is about outcomes, Stage III about the activities that produce them (p. 343).
Action matters only if it leads to outcomes, and outcomes only if they have a constructive impact, as Lacy's case shows (pp. 343-344).
Stage III has three tasks: III-A possible strategies, III-B best-fit strategies, III-C plans; planning is not action, and without action a plan is a wish list (p. 344).
Mara's goals are a supportive community, a better career and preparing to leave her parents if necessary (pp. 345-346).
Strategies are actions that achieve goals; developing them is liberating and builds self-efficacy (p. 346).
Helpers stimulate divergent thinking through focused brainstorming and 'prompt and fade', keeping the client in the driver's seat (pp. 346-348).
Frameworks of resources (individuals, models, communities, places, things, organisations, programs) generate strategies, as in Jackson's case; Box 13.1 gives questions (pp. 349-351).
Skills training, Carkhuff's 'training as treatment', is a key strategy when clients lack life skills (pp. 351-352).
Bud reached emotional stability through two best-fit strategies: finding support and helping others (pp. 352-353).
Strategies should be specific, robust, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective and value-consistent (Stacy, Desmond, the priest) (pp. 353-356).
Clients may sample strategies before choosing and weigh them with the balance-sheet method, best used flexibly as a source of probes (pp. 356-358).
Helpers must help clients link strategies to action; Clint's 'experiment' let him learn by acting (pp. 358-359).
Shadow side: Goslin's decision pitfalls and three risk pitfalls (wishful thinking, playing it safe, avoiding the worst outcome); the ideal balances risk and probability (pp. 359-361).
Task III-C organises strategies into a sequenced plan; Frank's lack of a plan cost him the presidency (pp. 361-362).
Plans build discipline, keep steps bite-size, prompt better strategies, test goals, reveal resources and uncover obstacles (pp. 362-364).
A well-shaped plan states what to do, in what order and when; subgoals help with complex goals (Harriet, Frank revisited, Box 13.3) (pp. 364-366).
Humanising principles: planning mentality from the start, adapt to client style, outline a plan for the client to tailor, and develop contingency plans (pp. 366-370).
Ready-made programmes include ESTs (e.g. Barlow's unified protocol) and well-being programmes; Egan favours a both-and approach and stresses that talk is not change (pp. 370-372).

assessment.q: Which question belongs to Task III-B?
options: What kind of actions will help me get what I need and want?
What actions are best for me?
What should I do first, second?
assessment.explain: Task III-B is about best-fit strategies: 'What actions are best for me?' (p. 344).

assessment.q: Without action, Egan says a programme for constructive change is:
options: Nothing more than a wish list
assessment.explain: Planning for action must not be confused with action itself (p. 344).

assessment.q: Which bias is listed in Chapter 2 as a key value, explaining why this chapter matters?
assessment.explain: Strategies are actions; that is why a bias toward action is a key value (p. 346).

assessment.q: Mara's brainstorming of ways to build a social life is notable because:
options: She took two weeks, noted ideas as they came, and acted on some at once
Carlos wrote the list for her
assessment.explain: She kept a notepad for a couple of weeks and joined LinkedIn, attended an alumni event and arranged a camp visit (p. 347).

assessment.q: In Jackson's case, the Internet chat room for cancer patients was classified under:
assessment.explain: Egan calls it a 'high-tech place' where Jackson could at times become a helper (p. 350).

assessment.q: Jerzy and Zelda's problems mainly stemmed from lack of:
options: Interpersonal communication skills, developmental understanding and problem-solving skills
assessment.explain: They lacked communication skills, working knowledge of each other's developmental needs and problem-solving skills (p. 351).

assessment.q: Which list correctly gives Egan's criteria for strategies?
options: Specific, robust, prudent, realistic, sustainable, flexible, cost-effective, value-consistent
assessment.explain: Strategies, like goals, should meet these eight criteria (p. 353).

assessment.q: Stacy's improvement came from:
options: A comprehensive social-learning programme with cognitive restructuring, social-skills training and behavioural interventions
assessment.explain: A new psychiatrist placed her in a social-learning programme and she was discharged within six months (p. 354).

assessment.q: Bud's catatonic attack occurred on the day of:
options: The change from daylight saving to standard time
assessment.explain: This ordinary change seemed to be the last straw (p. 352).

assessment.q: Karen's counsellor in the balance-sheet example was:
assessment.explain: Joan helped Karen weigh the residential programme with the balance sheet (p. 357).

assessment.q: Liam, who drops hints and jokes instead of raising concerns with his boss, illustrates:
assessment.explain: He chooses low-risk actions with limited chance of success and does not see how safe he is playing it (p. 360).

assessment.q: Who described three ways clients deal with risk and probability?
assessment.explain: Gelatt, Varenhorst and Carey (1972) named wishful thinking, playing it safe and avoiding the worst outcome (p. 359).

assessment.q: Which advantage of planning does Ernesto's case illustrate?
assessment.explain: Planning his social life revealed his shame, which became central to healing (p. 364).

assessment.q: For Bud's self-help organisation, 'charter in place' was:
options: A subgoal leading to his main goal
assessment.explain: Setting up a test group and establishing a charter were subgoals (p. 364).

assessment.q: Gitta embraced detailed planning mainly because:
options: It fitted her style; she had run her household that way for years
assessment.explain: The process was familiar though the content was new (p. 368).

options: What can I do that will add most value?
How can I complete a full formal plan?
assessment.explain: With limited sessions, extensive planning is impossible (p. 369).

options: Include blame reduction and redefinition of beauty
Insist on a detailed programme from the first session
Add detail as Katrina got involved
assessment.explain: She presented a simple outline and added detail only gradually (p. 369).

assessment.explain: Egan uses this to show goals may need to change (p. 370).

assessment.q: Egan's position on ESTs versus common-factors helping is:
options: A both-and approach based on the client's needs
assessment.explain: It is not either-or; use whatever helps clients (p. 371).

assessment.explain: Egan gives the figure as over 30% (p. 372).
